</head> <body> <div class="container-fluid main-container"> <div id="header"> <h1 class="title toc-ignore">GLM-examples</h1> </div> <div id="TOC"> <ul> <li> <a href="#models-for-proportion-binomial-glms" id="toc-models-for-proportion-binomial-glms">Models for proportion: Binomial GLMs</a> <ul> <li><a href="#examples" id="toc-examples">Examples</a></li> <li><a href="#binomial-pmf-in-edm-form" id="toc-binomial-pmf-in-edm-form">Binomial PMF in EDM form</a></li> <li><a href="#link-functions" id="toc-link-functions">Link Functions</a></li> <li><a href="#odds-odds-ratios-logit-link" id="toc-odds-odds-ratios-logit-link">Odds, Odds Ratios & Logit Link</a></li> <li><a href="#median-effective-dose-ed50" id="toc-median-effective-dose-ed50">Median Effective Dose: ED50</a></li> <li><a href="#overdispersion" id="toc-overdispersion">Overdispersion</a></li> <li> <a href="#no-goodness-of-fit-for-binary-data" id="toc-no-goodness-of-fit-for-binary-data">No goodness-of-fit for binary data</a> </li> <li><a href="#case-study" id="toc-case-study">case study</a></li> </ul> </li> <li> <a href="#models-for-counts" id="toc-models-for-counts">Models for counts</a> <ul> <li><a href="#example" id="toc-example">Example</a></li> <li><a href="#introduction-model-summary" id="toc-introduction-model-summary">introduction & model summary</a></li> <li> <a href="#action" id="toc-action">action</a> <ul> <li> <a href="#contingency-tables-log-linear-models" id="toc-contingency-tables-log-linear-models">contingency tables: log-linear models</a> </li> <li><a href="#higher-order-tables" id="toc-higher-order-tables">higher-order tables</a></li> </ul> </li> <li> <a href="#overdispersin-for-poisson-glms" id="toc-overdispersin-for-poisson-glms">overdispersin for Poisson GLMs</a> <ul> <li> <a href="#remedy-for-overdispersion-negative-binomial-glms" id="toc-remedy-for-overdispersion-negative-binomial-glms">remedy for overdispersion: negative binomial GLMs</a> </li> <li> <a href="#remedy-for-overdispersion-quasi-poisson-glms" id="toc-remedy-for-overdispersion-quasi-poisson-glms">remedy for overdispersion: quasi-Poisson GLMs</a> </li> </ul> </li> <li><a href="#case-study-1" id="toc-case-study-1">case study</a></li> </ul> </li> <li> <a href="#models-for-positive-continuous-data" id="toc-models-for-positive-continuous-data">Models for positive continuous data</a> <ul> <li><a href="#modeling-positive-continuous-data" id="toc-modeling-positive-continuous-data">modeling positive continuous data</a></li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="models-for-proportion-binomial-glms" class="section level1 tabset"> <h1 class="tabset">Models for proportion: Binomial GLMs</h1> <div id="examples" class="section level2"> <h2>Examples</h2> <ul> <li> A study produced similar symptoms by exposing volunteers’ lower bodies to negative air pressure, likewise decreasing oxygen to the brain. The data record the ages of eight volunteers and whether they showed syncopal blackout-related signs (pallor, sweating, slow heartbeat, unconsciousness) during an 18 min period. Does resistance to blackout decrease with age? <ul> <li> The explanatory variable is Age. The response variable is Signs, coded as 1 if the subject showed blackout-related signs and 0 otherwise. The response variable is binary, taking only two distinct values, and no transformation can change that. </li> </ul> </li> <li> Second example, the response variable is the number of damaged O-rings out of six for each of the previous 23 launches with data available, so only seven values are possible for the response. No transformation can change this. </li> <li> Rather than linear regression, a more sensible model would be to use a binomial distribution with mean proportion <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span> for modelling the <strong>proportion</strong> <span class="math inline">\(y\)</span> of O-rings damaged out of m at various temperatures x. </li> </ul> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \log \frac{\mu}{1-\mu}=\beta_0+\beta_1x \]</span> combining the systematic and random components, a possible model for the data is: </p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} ym \sim \text{Bin}(\mu,m) \quad &(\text{random component})\\ \log \frac{\mu}{1-\mu}=\beta_0+\beta_1x \quad &(\text{systematic component}) \end{cases} \]</span> </p> </div> <div id="binomial-pmf-in-edm-form" class="section level2"> <h2>Binomial PMF in EDM form</h2> <p> the outcome of many studies is a proportion y of a total number m: the proportion of individuals having a diseasel; the proportion of voters who vote in favor of a particular election candidate; … each case, the m individuals in each group are assumed to be <strong>independent</strong> and each individual can be classified into one of <strong>two possible outcomes</strong>. </p> <p><span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{P}(y|\mu, m)={m \choose my}\mu^{my}(1-\mu)^{m(1-y)} \]</span></p> <p> where <span class="math inline">\(m\)</span> is known and <span class="math inline">\(\phi=1, 0<\mu<1\)</span>. For binomial GLMs, the use of quantile residuals is strongly recommended for diagnostic analysis. </p> <p>Binomial responses may be specified in the <code>glm()</code> formula in one of three ways:</p> <ul> <li> The response can be supplied as the observed proportions <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span>, when the sample sizes <span class="math inline">\(m_i\)</span> are supplied as the weights in the call to <code>glm()</code>. </li> <li> The response can be given as a two-column array, the columns giving the numbers of successes and failures respectively in each group of size <span class="math inline">\(m_i\)</span>. The prior weights <code>weights</code> do not need to be supplied. </li> <li> The response can be given as a factor or as a logical. This specification is useful if the data have one row for each observation. </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code>data(turbines)

tur.m1 <- glm( Fissures/Turbines ~ Hours, family=binomial,
               weights=Turbines, data=turbines) # 1st 
tur.m2 <- glm( cbind(Fissures, Turbines-Fissures) ~ Hours,
               family=binomial, data=turbines) # 2nd
coef(tur.m1) </code></pre> <pre><code>##   (Intercept)         Hours 
## -3.9235965551  0.0009992372</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>coef(tur.m2)</code></pre> <pre><code>##   (Intercept)         Hours 
## -3.9235965551  0.0009992372</code></pre> </div> <div id="link-functions" class="section level2"> <h2>Link Functions</h2> <p>to ensure <span class="math inline">\(0<\mu<1\)</span>, possible choice of link function for binomial GLMs are:</p> <ul> <li> <code>logit</code> link function, which is the canonical link function for the binomial distribution and the default link function in R: </li> </ul> <p><span class="math display">\[ \eta=\log \frac{\mu}{1-\mu}=logit(\mu) \]</span></p> <p> -<code>probit</code> link function: <span class="math inline">\(\eta=\Phi^{-1}(\mu)=probit(\mu)\)</span>, where <span class="math inline">\(\Phi(\cdot)\)</span> is the CDF for the normal distribution. This link function is specified in R as <code>link="probit</code>. </p> <ul> <li> complementary log-log link function: <span class="math inline">\(\eta=\log \{-\log (1-\mu)\}\)</span>, specified as <code>link="cloglog"</code>. </li> <li> log link: used for modeling risk ratios or relative risks, an approximation to logit link when <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span> is small. </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code>tr.logit <- glm( Fissures/Turbines ~ Hours, data=turbines,
                 family=binomial, weights=Turbines)
tr.probit <- update( tr.logit, family=binomial(link="probit") )
tr.cll <- update( tr.logit, family=binomial(link="cloglog") )

tr.array <- rbind( coef(tr.logit), coef(tr.probit), coef(tr.cll))
tr.array <- cbind( tr.array, 
                   c(deviance(tr.logit), 
                     deviance(tr.probit), 
                     deviance(tr.cll)) )
colnames(tr.array) <- c("Intercept", "Hours","Residual dev.")
rownames(tr.array) <- c("Logit","Probit","Comp log-log")
tr.array</code></pre> <pre><code>##              Intercept        Hours Residual dev.
## Logit        -3.923597 0.0009992372     10.331466
## Probit       -2.275807 0.0005783211      9.814837
## Comp log-log -3.603280 0.0008104936     12.227914</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>newHrs <- seq( 0, 5000, length=100)
newdf <- data.frame(Hours=newHrs)
newP.logit <- predict( tr.logit, newdata=newdf, type="response")
newP.probit <- predict( tr.probit, newdata=newdf, type="response")
newP.cll <- predict( tr.cll, newdata=newdf, type="response")

plot( Fissures/Turbines ~ Hours, data=turbines, 
      pch=19, las=1,
      xlim=c(0, 5000), ylim=c(0, 0.7),
      xlab="Hours run", ylab="Proportion with fissures")
lines( newP.logit ~ newHrs, lty=1, lwd=2)
lines( newP.probit ~ newHrs, lty=2, lwd=2)
lines( newP.cll ~ newHrs, lty=4, lwd=2)
legend("topleft", lwd=2, lty=c(1, 2, 4),
       legend=c("Logit","Probit","Comp. log-log"))</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> </div> <div id="odds-odds-ratios-logit-link" class="section level2"> <h2>Odds, Odds Ratios & Logit Link</h2> <pre class="r"><code>LogOdds <- predict( tr.logit )
odds <- exp( LogOdds )
plot( LogOdds ~ turbines$Hours, type="l", las=1,
      xlim=c(0, 5000), ylim=c(-5, 1),
      ylab="Empirical Log-odds", xlab="Run-time (in hours)" )


my <- turbines$Fissures
m <- turbines$Turbines
EmpiricalOdds <- (my + 0.5)/(m - my + 0.5) # empirical log-odds: avoid log of 0s
points( log(EmpiricalOdds) ~ turbines$Hours)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>plot( odds ~ turbines$Hours, las=1, xlim=c(0, 5000), ylim=c(0, 2),
      type="l", ylab="Odds", xlab="Run-time (in hours)")
points( EmpiricalOdds ~ turbines$Hours)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <p><span class="math display">\[ \log \frac{\mu}{1-\mu}=\log-\text{odds}=\beta_0+\beta_1x \]</span></p> <p> where x is a dummy variable taking the values 0 or 1. From this equation, we see that the odds of observing a success when <span class="math inline">\(x = 0\)</span> is <span class="math inline">\(\exp(\beta_0)\)</span>, and the odds of observing a success when <span class="math inline">\(x = 1\)</span> is <span class="math inline">\(\exp(β0 + β1) = \exp(\beta_0) \exp(\beta_1)\)</span>. The ratio of these two odds is <span class="math inline">\(\exp(\beta_1)\)</span>. This means that the odds of a success occurring when <span class="math inline">\(x = 1\)</span> is <span class="math inline">\(\exp(\beta_1)\)</span> times greater than when <span class="math inline">\(x = 0\)</span>. This ratio is called the <strong>odds ratio</strong>, often written OR. </p> </div> <div id="median-effective-dose-ed50" class="section level2"> <h2>Median Effective Dose: ED50</h2> <p> Binomial GLMs are commonly used to examine the relationship between the dose d of a drug and the proportion y of insects that survive. These models are called <strong>dose-response models</strong>. ED50: the dose of poison affecting <span class="math inline">\(50\%\)</span> of the insects. By definition, <span class="math inline">\(\mu=0.5\)</span> at the ED50. For a binomial GLM using logit link function, <span class="math inline">\(\eta=\log(\mu/(1-\mu))=0\)</span> when <span class="math inline">\(\mu=0.5\)</span>, where <span class="math inline">\(\eta=\beta_0+\beta_1d\)</span> and d is the dose. Solving for dose d gives that ED50 <span class="math inline">\(=-\hat{\beta_0}/\hat{\beta_1}\)</span>. </p> </div> <div id="overdispersion" class="section level2"> <h2>Overdispersion</h2> <p> For a binomial distribution, var<span class="math inline">\([y]=\mu(1-\mu)\)</span>. The amount of variation in the data can exceed this value, called <code>overdispersion</code>. Consequences are standard errors by GLM are underestimated, and tests on predictors will generally be more significant leading to overly complex models. </p> <p> Overdispersion can be detected by goodness-of-fit test. Lack of fit may be caused by an inadequate model. But if all possible predictors are already in the model and no outliers exist when lack of fit persists ,then overdispersion is the alternative interpretation. </p> <p> Overdispersion arises in two cases: the probabilities <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i\)</span> are not constant between observations; the <span class="math inline">\(m_i\)</span> cases, of which observations <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span> is a proportion, are not independent. </p> <p><code>Quasi-binomial</code> GLMs are the remedies for overdispersion.</p> <p> Example: Since seedsare usually planted together in common plots, it is highly possible that they might interact or be affected by common causes; in other words we might well expect seeds to be positively correlated, leading to overdispersion. </p> <pre class="r"><code>data(germ)
gm.m1 <- glm(Germ/Total ~ Seeds * Extract, family=binomial,
             data=germ, weights=Total)
printCoefmat(coef(summary(gm.m1)))</code></pre> <pre><code>##                           Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)  
## (Intercept)               -0.41224    0.18418 -2.2383  0.02520 *
## SeedsOA75                 -0.14593    0.22317 -0.6539  0.51318  
## ExtractCucumber            0.54008    0.24981  2.1619  0.03062 *
## SeedsOA75:ExtractCucumber  0.77810    0.30643  2.5392  0.01111 *
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>anova(gm.m1, test="Chisq")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: binomial, link: logit
## 
## Response: Germ/Total
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##               Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev Pr(>Chi)    
## NULL                             20     98.719             
## Seeds          1    2.544        19     96.175  0.11070    
## Extract        1   56.489        18     39.686 5.65e-14 ***
## Seeds:Extract  1    6.408        17     33.278  0.01136 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>c( deviance(gm.m1), df.residual(gm.m1) )</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 33.27779 17.00000</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># diagnostic plot
qres <- qresid(gm.m1)
qqnorm(qres, las=1)
abline(0, 1)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code># deviance residual vs fitted values
scatter.smooth( qres ~ fitted( gm.m1 ), 
                col="grey", las=1, 
                ylab="Standardized residuals", 
                xlab="Fitted values")</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> the residual deviance is much larger than the residual degrees of freedom; from QQ-plot no large residuals present that would suggest outliers; influential observations cannot be an issue. So <strong>overdispersion</strong> is present. </p> <pre class="r"><code>gm.od <- update(gm.m1, family=quasibinomial)
anova(gm.od, test="F")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: quasibinomial, link: logit
## 
## Response: Germ/Total
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##               Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev       F    Pr(>F)    
## NULL                             20     98.719                      
## Seeds          1    2.544        19     96.175  1.3665   0.25854    
## Extract        1   56.489        18     39.686 30.3407 3.839e-05 ***
## Seeds:Extract  1    6.408        17     33.278  3.4418   0.08099 .  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <p> The quasi-binomial analysis of deviance suggests that only Extract is significant in the model, so germination frequency differs by root stock but not by seed type, unlike the binomial glm which showed a significant Extract by Seeds interaction. </p> <p> The binomial and quasi-binomial glms give identical coefficient estimates, but the standard errors from the quasi-binomial GLM are <span class="math inline">\(\sqrt{\phi}\)</span> times those from the binomial model: </p> <pre class="r"><code>sqrt(summary(gm.od)$dispersion)</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 1.36449</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>beta <- coef(summary(gm.m1))[,"Estimate"]
m1.se <- coef(summary(gm.m1))[,"Std. Error"]
od.se <- coef(summary(gm.od))[,"Std. Error"]
data.frame(Estimate=beta, Binom.SE=m1.se,
           Quasi.SE=od.se, Ratio=od.se/m1.se)</code></pre> <pre><code>##                             Estimate  Binom.SE  Quasi.SE   Ratio
## (Intercept)               -0.4122448 0.1841784 0.2513095 1.36449
## SeedsOA75                 -0.1459269 0.2231659 0.3045076 1.36449
## ExtractCucumber            0.5400782 0.2498130 0.3408672 1.36449
## SeedsOA75:ExtractCucumber  0.7781037 0.3064332 0.4181249 1.36449</code></pre> </div> <div id="no-goodness-of-fit-for-binary-data" class="section level2"> <h2>No goodness-of-fit for binary data</h2> <p>For binary data, likelihood ratio tests and score tests should be used, making sure that p’ is much smaller than n.</p> </div> <div id="case-study" class="section level2"> <h2>case study</h2> <p> an experiment exposed batches of insects to various deposits of insecticides. The proportion of insects y killed after six days of exposure in each batch of size m is potentially a function of the dose of insecticide and the type of insecticide. </p> <pre class="r"><code>data(deposit)
deposit$Prop <- deposit$Killed / deposit$Number


plot( Prop ~ Deposit, type="n", las=1, ylim=c(0, 1),
      data=deposit, main="Proportion of\ninsects killed",
      xlab="Deposit (in mg)", ylab="Proportion killed")
points( Prop ~ Deposit, pch="A", subset=(Insecticide=="A"), data=deposit)
points( Prop ~ Deposit, pch="B", subset=(Insecticide=="B"), data=deposit)
points( Prop ~ Deposit, pch="C", subset=(Insecticide=="C"), data=deposit)

## 
## Model 1: Killed/Number ~ logDep + Insecticide - 1
## Model 2: Killed/Number ~ poly(logDep, 2) + Insecticide
##   Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi)   
## 1        14     23.385                        
## 2        13     15.090  1   8.2949 0.003976 **
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <p> the quadratic model is a statistically significantly improvement; no evidence exists to support overdispersion: the deviance is 15 and df is 13. </p> </div> </div> <div id="models-for-counts" class="section level1 tabset"> <h1 class="tabset">Models for counts</h1> <div id="example" class="section level2"> <h2>Example</h2> <ul> <li> quoting the number of diseased people in various cities is an unfair comparison, as some cities have a far larger population; comparing the number of people with the disease per unit population is a fairer comparison. <ul> <li>the disease rate is often more suitable for modelling than the actual number of people with the disease.</li> <li>Poisson glms are more convenient when the populations are large and the rates are relatively small.</li> </ul> </li> <li> A study of the habitats of the noisy miner (a small but aggressive native Australian bird) counted the number of noisy miners y and the number of eucalypt trees x in two-hectare buloke woodland transects. Buloke woodland patches with more eucalypts tend to have more noisy miners <ul> <li> The number of noisy miners is more variable where more eucalypts are present. Between 0 and 10 eucalypts, the number of noisy miners is almost always zero; between 10 and 20 ucalypts, the number of noisy miners increases. This shows that the systematic relationship between the number of eucalypts and the number of noisy miners is not linear. </li> <li> Between 0 and 10 eucalypts, the number of noisy miners varies little. Between 10 and 20 eucalypts, a larger amount of variation exists in the number of noisy miners. This shows that the randomness does not have constant variance. </li> <li>the variation in the data may be modelled using a Poisson distribution.</li> <li> A possible model for the systematic component is <span class="math inline">\(\log \mu = \beta_0+\beta_1x\)</span>, where x is the number of eucalypt trees at a given site, and μ is the expected number of noisy miners. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} y \sim \text{Pois}(\mu) \quad (\text{random component}) \\ \log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1x \quad (\text{systematic component}) \end{cases} \]</span> </p> </div> <div id="introduction-model-summary" class="section level2"> <h2>introduction & model summary</h2> <p> Poisson distribution is used to model counts, which has PMF: <span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{P}(y;\lambda)=\frac{\exp(-\lambda)\lambda^y}{y!} \]</span> The unit deviance for Poisson distribution is: <span class="math display">\[ d(y, \lambda)=2\{y\log\frac{y}{\lambda}-(y-\lambda)\} \]</span> and the residual deviance is <span class="math display">\[ D(y,\hat{\lambda})=\sum w_i d(y_i, \hat{\lambda}_i) \]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(w_i\)</span> are the prior weights. </p> </div> <div id="action" class="section level2"> <h2>action</h2> <p> model defined as <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} y \sim \text{Pois}(\mu) \quad (\text{random component}) \\ \log\mu=\log T+\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_j \quad (\text{systematic component}) \end{cases} \]</span> </p> <pre class="r"><code>data(danishlc)
danishlc$Rate <- danishlc$Cases / danishlc$Pop * 1000 # Rate per 1000
danishlc$Age <- ordered(danishlc$Age, # Ensure age-order is preserved
                        levels=c("40-54", "55-59", "60-64", "65-69", "70-74", ">74") )

danishlc$City <- abbreviate(danishlc$City, 1)  # Abbreviate city names
matplot( xtabs( Rate ~ Age+City, data=danishlc), pch=1:4, lty=1:4,
         type="b", lwd=2, col="black", axes=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 25),
         xlab="Age group", ylab="Cases/1000")
axis(side=1, at=1:6, labels=levels(danishlc$Age))
axis(side=2, las=1)
box()
legend("topleft", col="black", pch=1:4, lwd=2, lty=1:4, merge=FALSE,
       legend=c("Fredericia", "Horsens", "Kolding", "Vejle") )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>dlc.m1 <- glm( Cases ~ offset( log(Pop) ) + City * Age,
               family=poisson, data=danishlc)
anova(dlc.m1, test="Chisq")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: poisson, link: log
## 
## Response: Cases
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##          Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev Pr(>Chi)    
## NULL                        23    129.908             
## City      3    3.393        20    126.515  0.33495    
## Age       5  103.068        15     23.447  < 2e-16 ***
## City:Age 15   23.447         0      0.000  0.07509 .  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <p>city seems not significant; alternatively, consider age as continuous and a quadratic term:</p> <pre class="r"><code>dlc.m2 <- update(dlc.m1, . ~ offset(log(Pop)) + Age )

danishlc$AgeNum <- rep( c(40, 55, 60, 65, 70, 75), 4)
dlc.m3 <- update(dlc.m1, . ~ offset( log(Pop) ) + AgeNum)
dlc.m4 <- update(dlc.m3, . ~ offset( log(Pop) ) + poly(AgeNum, 2) )

anova( dlc.m3, dlc.m4, test="Chisq")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model 1: Cases ~ AgeNum + offset(log(Pop))
## Model 2: Cases ~ poly(AgeNum, 2) + offset(log(Pop))
##   Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance  Pr(>Chi)    
## 1        22     48.968                          
## 2        21     32.500  1   16.468 4.948e-05 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <p>now compare 4 models using AIC/BIC:</p> <pre class="r"><code>c( "With interaction"=AIC(dlc.m1), "Without interaction"=AIC(dlc.m2),
"Age (numerical)"=AIC(dlc.m3), "Age (numerical; quadratic)"=AIC(dlc.m4) )</code></pre> <pre><code>##           With interaction        Without interaction 
##                   144.3880                   136.6946 
##            Age (numerical) Age (numerical; quadratic) 
##                   149.3556                   134.8876</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># goodness-of-fit test
D.m2 <- deviance(dlc.m2)
df.m2 <- df.residual( dlc.m2 )
c( Dev=D.m2, df=df.m2, P = pchisq( D.m2, df.m2, lower = FALSE) )</code></pre> <pre><code>##         Dev          df           P 
## 28.30652745 18.00000000  0.05754114</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>D.m4 <- deviance(dlc.m4)
df.m4 <- df.residual( dlc.m4 )
c( Dev=D.m4, df=df.m4, P = pchisq( D.m4, df.m4, lower = FALSE) )</code></pre> <pre><code>##         Dev          df           P 
## 32.49959158 21.00000000  0.05206888</code></pre> <p>Both models are reasonably adequate. now consider diagnostic plots:</p> <pre class="r"><code># factor age model
scatter.smooth( rstandard(dlc.m2) ~ sqrt(fitted(dlc.m2)),
                ylab="Standardized residuals", xlab="Sqrt(Fitted values)",
                main="Factor age model", las=1 )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>plot( cooks.distance(dlc.m2), type="h", las=1, main="Cook's D", ylab="Cook's distance, D")</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>qqnorm( qr<-qresid(dlc.m2), las=1 ); abline(0, 1)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code># quadratic age model
scatter.smooth( rstandard(dlc.m4) ~ sqrt(fitted(dlc.m4)),
                ylab="Standardized residuals", xlab="Sqrt(Fitted values)",
                main="Quadratic age model", las=1 )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>plot( cooks.distance(dlc.m4), type="h", las=1, main="Cook's D", ylab="Cook's distance, D")</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>qqnorm( qr<-qresid(dlc.m4), las=1 ); abline(0, 1)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <p>Two models are reasonable. But we prefer model 2 since model 4 has three influential obs compared to the rest and model 2 is simpler.</p> <div id="contingency-tables-log-linear-models" class="section level3"> <h3>contingency tables: log-linear models</h3> <div id="systematic-component" class="section level4"> <h4>systematic component</h4> <ul> <li> two-way contingency table: factor A with I levels and factor B with J levels <ul> <li> <span class="math inline">\(y_{ij}\)</span> refers to the observed count in row i and column j, <span class="math inline">\(i=1,2,\dots, I, j=1,2,\dots,J\)</span> </li> <li> let <span class="math inline">\(\mu_{ij}\)</span> be the expected count in cell (i,j), <span class="math inline">\(\pi_{ij}\)</span> be the expected probability that an observation is in cell (i,j), and <span class="math inline">\(\mu_{ij}=m\pi_{ij}\)</span> where m is the total number of obs. </li> <li> let <span class="math inline">\(m_{i \cdot}\)</span> be the sum of counts in row i over all columns, <span class="math inline">\(m_{\cdot j}\)</span> be the sum of counts in column j over all rows. -<span class="math inline">\(\pi_{ij}=\pi_{i \cdot}\pi_{\cdot j}\)</span> if factors A and B are independent; then <span class="math inline">\(\mu_{ij}=m\pi_{i\cdot}\pi_{\cdot j}\)</span> </li> <li>taking logarithms: <span class="math inline">\(\log \mu_{ij}=\log m+\log \pi_{i \cdot} + \log \pi_{\cdot j}\)</span></li> <li> the probabilities <span class="math inline">\(\pi_{i \cdot}\)</span> depend on which row the observation is in; the probabilities <span class="math inline">\(\pi_{\cdot j}\)</span> depend on which colum the obs. is in </li> </ul> </li> <li> example by simplest contingency table <ul> <li>to test for independence of row and column factors</li> <li> a probabilistic model for the counts is needed. a complete model for the data depends on how the sample of individuals was collected. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code>Counts <- c(263, 258, 151, 222)
Att <- gl(2, 2, 4, labels=c("For", "Against") )
Inc <- gl(2, 1, 4, labels=c("High", "Low") )
data.frame( Counts, Att, Inc)</code></pre> <pre><code>##   Counts     Att  Inc
## 1    263     For High
## 2    258     For  Low
## 3    151 Against High
## 4    222 Against  Low</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>gm.table <- xtabs( Counts ~ Att + Inc )
gm.table</code></pre> <pre><code>##          Inc
## Att       High Low
##   For      263 258
##   Against  151 222</code></pre> </div> <div id="random-component" class="section level4"> <h4>random component</h4> <p>sample scheme by presetting row/column margins</p> <ul> <li> m obs. are randomly allocated to factor A and B as they arrive; neither row nor column total were fixed <ul> <li>no margins were fixed and no limit on how large the number of counts can be</li> <li> if the total number of individuals observed follow a Poisson distribution and individuals are independent, then each of the counts in the contingency table follow a Poisson fdistribution </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p> the log-likelihood function for the <span class="math inline">\(2 \times 2\)</span> table is given as <span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{L}(\mu;y)=\sum_{i=1}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{2}(-\mu_{ij}+y_{ij}\log \mu_{ij}) \]</span> </p> <pre class="r"><code>gm.1 <- glm( Counts ~ Att + Inc, family=poisson)
anova( gm.1, test="Chisq")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: poisson, link: log
## 
## Response: Counts
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##      Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev  Pr(>Chi)    
## NULL                     3     38.260              
## Att   1  24.6143         2     13.646 7.003e-07 ***
## Inc   1   4.8769         1      8.769   0.02722 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>coef(gm.1)</code></pre> <pre><code>## (Intercept)  AttAgainst      IncLow 
##   5.4859102  -0.3341716   0.1479201</code></pre> <p> the model has the systematic component <span class="math inline">\(\log \mu_{ij}=5.486-0.334x_1 + 0.1479x_2\)</span> where <span class="math inline">\(x_1=1\)</span> for obs located at the second row i.e., <span class="math inline">\(i=2\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(x_2=1\)</span> if obs at second column i.e., <span class="math inline">\(j=2\)</span>. unlogging gets us the systematic component in their original units. </p> <p>to test for the interaction between factor A and B:</p> <pre class="r"><code>gm.int <- glm( Counts ~ Att * Inc, family=poisson)
anova( gm.int, test="Chisq")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: poisson, link: log
## 
## Response: Counts
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##         Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev  Pr(>Chi)    
## NULL                        3     38.260              
## Att      1  24.6143         2     13.646 7.003e-07 ***
## Inc      1   4.8769         1      8.769  0.027218 *  
## Att:Inc  1   8.7686         0      0.000  0.003065 ** 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <p> The analysis of deviance table shows the interaction term is necessary in the model. the data suggest an association between A and B. </p> <ul> <li>the total number of obs. m was fixed, i.e., the grand total is fixed</li> </ul> <p>instead of a Poisson distribution, a multi-nomial distribution is appropriate.</p> <p> the log-likelihood function for the <span class="math inline">\(2 \times 2\)</span> table is given as <span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{L}(\mu;y)=\sum_{i=1}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{2}y_{ij}\log \mu_{ij} \]</span> Estimating <span class="math inline">\(\mu_{ij}\)</span> by maximizing the log-likelihood for the multinomial distribution constrained by <span class="math inline">\(\sum_{i=1}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{2}y_{ij}=m\)</span>. The Poisson model, conditioning on the grand total, is equivalent to a multinomial model. </p> <ul> <li> row totals were fixed, and obs. were allocated to column factor within each level of row factor <ul> <li>or column totals are fixed</li> <li>the residuals deviance are exactly the same as above, Poisson dist. is applicable here</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="three-way-contingency-tables" class="section level4"> <h4>three-way contingency tables</h4> <pre class="r"><code>data(kstones)

ks.mutind <- glm( Counts ~ Size + Method + Outcome, family=poisson, data=kstones) # mutual indep.
ks.SM <- glm( Counts ~ Size * Method + Outcome, family=poisson, data=kstones )  # partial independence
ks.SO <- update(ks.SM, . ~ Size * Outcome + Method)
ks.OM <- update(ks.SM, . ~ Outcome * Method + Size)
ks.noMO <- glm( Counts ~ Size * (Method + Outcome), family=poisson, data=kstones ) # conditional indep.
ks.noOS <- update(ks.noMO, . ~ Method * (Outcome + Size) )
ks.noMS <- update(ks.noMO, . ~ Outcome * (Method + Size) )
ks.no3 <- glm( Counts ~ Size*Method*Outcome - Size:Method:Outcome, family=poisson, data=kstones ) # uniform assoc.
ks.all <- glm( Counts ~ Size * Method * Outcome, family=poisson, data=kstones ) # saturated model

# model comparison</code></pre> <ul> <li>Simpson’s Paradox</li> </ul> </div> </div> <div id="higher-order-tables" class="section level3"> <h3>higher-order tables</h3> <pre class="r"><code>data(dyouth)
dy.m1 <- glm( Obs ~ Age*Depression*Gender + Age*Group, data=dyouth, family=poisson)
anova(dy.m1, test="Chisq")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: poisson, link: log
## 
## Response: Obs
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##                       Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev  Pr(>Chi)    
## NULL                                     23     368.05              
## Age                    2   11.963        21     356.09  0.002525 ** 
## Depression             1  168.375        20     187.71 < 2.2e-16 ***
## Gender                 1   58.369        19     129.34 2.172e-14 ***
## Group                  1   69.104        18      60.24 < 2.2e-16 ***
## Age:Depression         2    3.616        16      56.62  0.163964    
## Age:Gender             2    3.631        14      52.99  0.162718    
## Depression:Gender      1    7.229        13      45.76  0.007175 ** 
## Age:Group              2   27.090        11      18.67 1.311e-06 ***
## Age:Depression:Gender  2    8.325         9      10.35  0.015571 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>Males <- subset(dyouth, Gender=="M")
Females <- subset(dyouth, Gender=="F")
table.M <- prop.table( xtabs(Obs~Age+Depression, data=Males), 1)
table.F <- prop.table( xtabs(Obs~Age+Depression, data=Females), 1)
round(table.F * 100) # FEMALES</code></pre> <pre><code>##        Depression
## Age      H  L
##   12-14 36 64
##   15-16 31 69
##   17-18 10 90</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>round(table.M * 100) # MALES</code></pre> <pre><code>##        Depression
## Age      H  L
##   12-14 20 80
##   15-16 12 88
##   17-18 20 80</code></pre> </div> </div> <div id="overdispersin-for-poisson-glms" class="section level2"> <h2>overdispersin for Poisson GLMs</h2> <p> for a Poisson dist., <span class="math inline">\(var[y]=E[y]\)</span>. in practise, however, the variance of the data exceeds <span class="math inline">\(E[y]\)</span>. this is called <strong>overdispersion</strong>. underdispersion occurs, but less commonly. </p> <p>reason for <strong>occurrence</strong>, <strong>effects</strong>, and <strong>detection</strong> of overdispersion:</p> <ul> <li> the mean retains some innate variability even after all predictors are fixed <ul> <li>clustered data</li> </ul> </li> <li>overdispersion may or may not affect the parameter estimates</li> <li> standard errors <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\beta}_j\)</span> are necessarily underestimated <ul> <li>tests on predictors generally appear to be more significant</li> <li>confidence intervals will be narrower</li> </ul> </li> <li> overdispersion can be detected by a goodness-of-fit test <ul> <li> if residual deviance and Pearson goodness-of-fit statistics are much larger than the residual df., then either the fitted model is inadequate or the data are overdispersed. </li> <li> if after fitting a saturated model and eliminating outliers, lack of fit remains meaning overdispersion is the alternative explanation. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code>data(pock)
plot( Count ~ jitter(log2(Dilution)), data=pock, las=1,
      xlab="Log (base 2) of dilution", ylab="Pock mark count")</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>mn <- with(pock, tapply(Count, log2(Dilution), mean) ) # Group means
vr <- with(pock, tapply(Count, log2(Dilution), var) ) # Group variances
plot( log(vr) ~ log(mn), las=1,
      xlab="Group mean", ylab="Group variance")</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>data.frame(mn, vr, ratio=vr/mn)</code></pre> <pre><code>##        mn         vr    ratio
## 0 186.625 1781.12500 9.543871
## 1 104.700  667.34444 6.373872
## 2  50.800  360.40000 7.094488
## 3  27.100  194.98889 7.195162
## 4   9.100   17.65556 1.940171</code></pre> <p> here we have an example of clustered data. the sample variance is much larger than the mean for each group, clear evidence of overdispersion. fitting a Poisson GLM shows substantial lack of fit: </p> <pre class="r"><code>m1 <- glm( Count ~ log2(Dilution), data=pock, family=poisson )
printCoefmat(coef(summary(m1)))</code></pre> <pre><code>##                 Estimate Std. Error z value  Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)     5.267932   0.022552 233.596 < 2.2e-16 ***
## log2(Dilution) -0.680944   0.015443 -44.093 < 2.2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>X2 <- sum(residuals(m1, type="pearson")^2)
c(Df=df.residual(m1), Resid.Dev=deviance(m1), Pearson.X2=X2)</code></pre> <pre><code>##         Df  Resid.Dev Pearson.X2 
##    46.0000   290.4387   291.5915</code></pre> <div id="remedy-for-overdispersion-negative-binomial-glms" class="section level3"> <h3>remedy for overdispersion: negative binomial GLMs</h3> <p> we can model overdispersion by assuming a second layer of variability by allowing <span class="math inline">\(E[y_i]=\lambda_i\)</span> to be a random variable: <span class="math display">\[ \begin{aligned} y_i|\lambda_i \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda_i), \lambda_i \sim \text{Gamma}(\mu_i, \phi) \end{aligned} \]</span> by hierarchical mixtures of random variables, we can show that </p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ y_i \sim \text{NB}(\mu_i, k) \]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(k=1/\phi\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(var[y_i]=\mu_i+\phi\mu_i^2\)</span>. </p> <pre class="r"><code>library(MASS) # Provides the function glm.nb()
m.nb <- glm.nb( Count ~ log2(Dilution), data=pock ) # fitting a negativev binomial GLM on y
m.nb$theta # phi </code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 9.892894</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>m.nb <- glm.convert(m.nb)
printCoefmat(coef(summary(m.nb, dispersion=1)))</code></pre> <pre><code>##                Estimate Std. Error z value  Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)     5.33284    0.08786  60.697 < 2.2e-16 ***
## log2(Dilution) -0.72460    0.03886 -18.646 < 2.2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> </div> <div id="remedy-for-overdispersion-quasi-poisson-glms" class="section level3"> <h3>remedy for overdispersion: quasi-Poisson GLMs</h3> <ul> <li> <p> quasi-Poisson models keep the Poisson variance function <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu)=\mu\)</span> but allows a general dispersion parameter <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu_i)=\phi \mu_i, \phi > 1\)</span>. </p> </li> <li> <p>mean-variance relationshio</p> <ul> <li> As compared to negative binomial models that use a quadratic variance function <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu)=\mu+\phi \mu^2\)</span>, quasi-Poisson models use a linear variance function <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu_i)=\phi \mu_i\)</span>. </li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>quasi-Poisson models return identical parameter estimates as those from corresponding Poisson GLMs.</p> <ul> <li>identical fitted values returned since identical estimates</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>the standard errors are inflated by a factor of <span class="math inline">\(\sqrt{\phi}\)</span></p> </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code>m.qp <- glm( Count ~ log2(Dilution), data=pock, family="quasipoisson")
se.m1 <- coef(summary(m1))[, "Std. Error"]
se.qp <- coef(summary(m.qp))[, "Std. Error"]
data.frame(SE.Pois=se.m1, SE.Quasi=se.qp, ratio=se.qp/se.m1)</code></pre> <pre><code>##                   SE.Pois   SE.Quasi    ratio
## (Intercept)    0.02255150 0.05677867 2.517733
## log2(Dilution) 0.01544348 0.03888257 2.517733</code></pre> </div> </div> <div id="case-study-1" class="section level2"> <h2>case study</h2> <p> In a study of nesting female horseshoe crabs, each with an attached male, the number of other nearby male crabs (called satellites) were counted. The colour of the female, the condition of her spine, her carapace width, and her weight were also recorded. The purpose of the study is to understand the factors that attract satellite crabs. Are they more attracted to larger females? Does the condition or colour of the female play a role? </p> <pre class="r"><code>data(hcrabs)

hcrabs$Col <- ordered(hcrabs$Col, levels=c("LM", "M", "DM", "D"))
hcrabs$Spine <- ordered(hcrabs$Spine, levels=c("NoneOK", "OneOK", "BothOK"))

# EDA
with(hcrabs,{
      logSat <- log(Sat+1)
      plot( jitter(Sat) ~ Wt, ylab="Sat", las=1)
      plot( jitter(logSat) ~ log(Wt), ylab="log(Sat+1)", las=1)
      plot( logSat ~ Col, ylab="log(Sat+1)", las=1)
      plot( jitter(Sat) ~ Width, ylab="Sat", las=1)
      plot( jitter(logSat) ~ log(Width), ylab="log(Sat+1)", las=1)
      plot( logSat ~ Spine, ylab="log(Sat+1)", las=1)
      })</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>with(hcrabs,{
      plot( log(Wt) ~ log(Width), las=1 )
      plot( log(Wt) ~ Col, las=1 )
      plot( log(Wt) ~ Spine, las=1 )
      })</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> inter-correlation between weight and width was observed; crabs tend to cluster and not to be independent, hence overdispersion was expected: </p> <pre class="r"><code>cr.m1 <- glm(Sat ~ log(Wt) + log(Width) + Spine + Col, family=quasipoisson, data=hcrabs)
anova(cr.m1, test="F")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: quasipoisson, link: log
## 
## Response: Sat
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##            Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev       F    Pr(>F)    
## NULL                         172     632.79                      
## log(Wt)     1   83.084       171     549.71 25.9645 9.429e-07 ***
## log(Width)  1    0.007       170     549.70  0.0023    0.9621    
## Spine       2    1.125       168     548.58  0.1758    0.8389    
## Col         3    7.630       165     540.95  0.7948    0.4984    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># check overdispersion
deviance(cr.m1)</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 540.946</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>df.residual(cr.m1)</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 165</code></pre> <p> The residual deviance is more than three times the residual degrees of freedom, overdispersion was thus confirmed; only logWt turned out to be significant. </p> <p> The final step is to refit the quasi-Poisson model or Negative Binomial model with only logWt term and plot diagnostics to identify potential deviations. </p> </div> </div> <div id="models-for-positive-continuous-data" class="section level1 tabset"> <h1 class="tabset">Models for positive continuous data</h1> <div id="modeling-positive-continuous-data" class="section level2"> <h2>modeling positive continuous data</h2> <ul> <li>the boundary at zero limits the left tail of the distribution, thus introduces skewness</li> <li> variance approaches 0 as the mean approaches 0, producing interesting mean-variance relationship <ul> <li><span class="math inline">\(V(\mu)=\mu^2\)</span>: <strong>gamma</strong> distribution</li> <li><span class="math inline">\(V(\mu)=\mu^3\)</span>: <strong>inverse Gaussian</strong> distribution</li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p> pdf for a gamma dist. is given as <span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{P}(y;\alpha, \beta)=\frac{y^{\alpha-1}\exp(-y/\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\beta^{\alpha}}, y>0, \alpha>0, \beta>0 \]</span> </p> <p> where <span class="math inline">\(\alpha, \beta\)</span> are the shape and scale parameters, respectively. <span class="math inline">\(E[y]=\alpha \beta, var[y]=\alpha\beta^2\)</span>. the canonical link function for a gamma dist. is the inverse link function <span class="math inline">\(\eta=1/\mu\)</span>; however, the logarithmic link function is often used because it avoids the need for contrains on the linear predictor in view of <span class="math inline">\(\mu>0\)</span>. </p> <p>writing the gamma pdf in terms of <span class="math inline">\(\mu, \phi\)</span> gives:</p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{P}(y;\alpha, \beta)=\frac{y}{\phi\mu}^{1/\phi}\frac{1}{y}\exp(-\frac{y}{\phi\mu})\frac{1}{\Gamma(1/\phi)} \]</span> </p> <p> the variance function is <span class="math inline">\(V[\mu]=\mu^2\)</span>. the coefficient of variation (CV) is defined as the ratio of the variance to the mean squared which is a measurement of the relative variation in the data. Gamma dist. has a CV<span class="math inline">\(=1\)</span>. </p> <p>example modelling foliage biomass y as a function of tree trunk diameter d:</p> <pre class="r"><code>data(lime)
str(lime)</code></pre> <pre><code>## 'data.frame':    385 obs. of  4 variables:
##  $ Foliage: num  0.1 0.2 0.4 0.6 0.6 0.8 1 1.4 1.7 3.5 ...
##  $ DBH    : num  4 6 8 9.6 11.3 13.7 15.4 17.8 18 22 ...
##  $ Age    : int  38 38 46 44 60 56 72 74 68 79 ...
##  $ Origin : Factor w/ 3 levels "Coppice","Natural",..: 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 ...</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># Plot Foliage against DBH
plot(Foliage ~ DBH, type="n", las=1, xlab="DBH (in cm)", 
     ylab="Foliage biomass (in kg)",
     ylim = c(0, 15), xlim=c(0, 40), data=lime)
points(Foliage ~ DBH, data=subset(lime, Origin=="Coppice"),pch=1)
points(Foliage ~ DBH, data=subset(lime, Origin=="Natural"),pch=2)
points(Foliage ~ DBH, data=subset(lime, Origin=="Planted"),pch=3)
legend("topleft", pch=c(1, 2, 3), legend=c("Coppice", "Natural","Planted"))</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code># Plot Foliage against DBH, on log scale
plot( log(Foliage) ~ log(DBH), type="n", las=1,
      xlab="log of DBH (in cm)", ylab="log of Foliage biomass (in kg)",
      ylim = c(-5, 3), xlim=c(0, 4), data=lime)
points( log(Foliage) ~ log(DBH), data=subset(lime, Origin=="Coppice"),pch=1)
points( log(Foliage) ~ log(DBH), data=subset(lime, Origin=="Natural"),pch=2)
points( log(Foliage) ~ log(DBH), data=subset(lime, Origin=="Planted"),pch=3)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code># Plot Foliage against Age
plot(Foliage ~ Age, type="n", las=1,
     xlab="Age (in years)", ylab="Foliage biomass (in kg)",
     ylim = c(0, 15), xlim=c(0, 150), data=lime)
points(Foliage ~ Age, data=subset(lime, Origin=="Coppice"), pch=1)
points(Foliage ~ Age, data=subset(lime, Origin=="Natural"), pch=2)
points(Foliage ~ Age, data=subset(lime, Origin=="Planted"), pch=3)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code># Plot Foliage against Origin
plot( Foliage ~ Origin, data=lime, ylim=c(0, 15), las=1, ylab="Foliage biomass (in kg)")</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> the response is always positive; the variance in foliage biomass increases as the mean DBH increases; </p> </div> </div> </div> <script>
      // add bootstrap table styles to pandoc tables
      function bootstrapStylePandocTables() {
        $("tr.odd").parent("tbody").parent("table").addClass("table table-condensed");
      }
      $(document).ready(function () {
        bootstrapStylePandocTables();
      });
    </script> <script>
      $(document).ready(function () {
        window.buildTabsets("TOC");
      });

      $(document).ready(function () {
        $(".tabset-dropdown > .nav-tabs > li").click(function () {
          $(this).parent().toggleClass("nav-tabs-open");
        });
      });
    </script> <script>
      (function () {
        var script = document.createElement("script");
        script.type = "text/javascript";
        script.src = "https://mathjax.rstudio.com/latest/MathJax.js?config=TeX-AMS-MML_HTMLorMML";
        document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(script);
      })();
    </script> </body> </html>

      /**
       * jQuery Plugin: Sticky Tabs

      (function ($) {
        "use strict";
        $.fn.rmarkdownStickyTabs = function () {
          var context = this;
          // Show the tab corresponding with the hash in the URL, or the first tab
          var showStuffFromHash = function () {
            var hash = window.location.hash;
            var selector = hash ? 'a[href="' + hash + '"]' : "li.active > a";
            var $selector = $(selector, context);

              $selector.tab("show");

              $selector.parents(".section.tabset").each(function (i, elm) {
                var link = $('a[href="#' + $(elm).attr("id") + '"]');
                if (link.data("toggle") === "tab") {
                  link.tab("show");
                }
              });
            }
          };

          // Set the correct tab when the page loads
          showStuffFromHash(context);

          // Set the correct tab when a user uses their back/forward button
          $(window).on("hashchange", function () {
            showStuffFromHash(context);
          });

          // Change the URL when tabs are clicked
          $("a", context).on("click", function (e) {

      window.buildTabsets = function (tocID) {
        // build a tabset from a section div with the .tabset class
        function buildTabset(tabset) {

          var fade = tabset.hasClass("tabset-fade");
          var pills = tabset.hasClass("tabset-pills");
          var navClass = pills ? "nav-pills" : "nav-tabs";

          if (match === null) return;
          var tabsetLevel = Number(match[1]);
          var tabLevel = tabsetLevel + 1;

          // find all subheadings immediately below
          var tabs = tabset.find("div.section.level" + tabLevel);
          if (!tabs.length) return;

          // create tablist and tab-content elements
          var tabList = $('<ul class="nav ' + navClass + '" role="tablist"></ul>');
          $(tabs[0]).before(tabList);
          var tabContent = $('<div class="tab-content"></div>');
          $(tabs[0]).before(tabContent);

          // build the tabset
          var activeTab = 0;
          tabs.each(function (i) {
            // get the tab div

            // get the id then sanitize it for use with bootstrap tabs

          buildTabset($(tabsets[i]));
