class="section level2"> <h2>where linear regression fails</h2> <p> general linear regression models assume the variance is constant, possibly from a normal distribution. However, many data types exist for which the randomness is not constant, which fails least-squares estimation and makes other methods necessary. </p> <p>three specific situations where the variation is not constant and linear regression models fail:</p> <ul> <li> <p> the response <span class="math inline">\(y\)</span> is a proportion out of m binary trials ranging between 0 and 1: binomial distribution may be appropriate. <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} ym \sim \text{Bin}(\mu, m) \quad (\text{random component}) \\ \log\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}=\beta_0+\beta_1x \quad (\text{systematic component}) \end{cases} \]</span> </p> </li> <li><p>the response is a count: poisson distribution may be appropriate</p></li> </ul> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} y \sim \text{Pois}(\mu) \quad (\text{random component}) \\ \log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1x \quad (\text{systematic component}) \end{cases} \]</span> </p> <ul> <li>the response is positive continuous: right skewed, thus gamma and inverse Gaussian distribution may be appropriate</li> </ul> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} y \sim \text{Gamma}(\mu;\phi) \quad (\text{random component}) \\ \mu=\beta_0+\beta_1x \quad (\text{systematic component}) \end{cases} \]</span> </p> <p> in these situations, the relationship between y and the predictors is usually non-linear, and the response has boundaries so a linear relationship cannot apply for all values of the response. </p> <p>Exponential family are useful for most common types of data:</p> <ul> <li>continuous data over the entire real line may be modeled by the normal distribution</li> <li>proportion of a total number of counts may be modeled by the binomial distribution</li> <li>discrete count data may be modeled by the Poisson or negative binomial distribution</li> <li>continuous data over the positive real line may be modeled by the gamma and inverse Guassian distribution</li> <li>positive data with exact zeros may be modeled by a special case of Tweedie distribution.</li> </ul> </div> <div id="maximum-likelihood-method" class="section level2"> <h2>maximum likelihood method</h2> <ul> <li>least-squares is an appropriate criterion for fitting regression models to response data that are normally distributed.</li> <li> maximum-likelihood is an appropriate for estimating the parameters of non-normal models on binomial, Poisson or gamma distributed response. <ul> <li>can be applied whenever a specific probability distribution has been proposed for the data</li> <li>estimating unknown parameters by choosing those that maximize the probability density of the data</li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p> suppose <span class="math inline">\(y_1, \dots, y_n\)</span> are independent observations from an exponential distribution with scale parameter <span class="math inline">\(\theta\)</span>, with pdf <span class="math inline">\(P(y;\theta)=\theta\exp (-y\theta)\)</span>, the joint pdf/likelihood function of the data is <span class="math display">\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{P}(y_1, \dots, y_n|\theta)&=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{P}(y_i|\theta)=\theta^n\exp (-\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i \theta) \\ \mathcal{L}(\theta;y)&=n(\log \theta-\bar{y}\theta) \end{aligned} \]</span> It is easy to show that least squares is a special case of maximum likelihood: consider a normal linear regression model, <span class="math inline">\(y_i \sim N(\mu_i, \sigma^2)\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{1i}+\dots, \beta_px_{pi}\)</span>, normal pdf is given by <span class="math display">\[ f(y_i; \mu_i, \sigma^2)=(2 \pi \sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp\bigg \{-\frac{(y_i-\mu_i)^2}{2\sigma^2} \bigg \} \]</span> hence the log pdf for single obs. <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span> is given as<br/> <span class="math display">\[ \log f(y_i; \mu_i, \sigma^2)=-\frac{1}{2}\log(2 \pi \sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y_i-\mu_i)^2 \]</span> the log-likelihood function for the unknown parameters is given as <span class="math display">\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\beta_0, \dots, \beta_p, \sigma^2;y)&=-\frac{n}{2}\log(2 \pi \sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\mu_i)^2 \\ &=-\frac{n}{2}\log(2 \pi \sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \text{SS} \end{aligned} \]</span> to maximize the likelihood is the same as minimizing the sum of squares. hence maximum likelihood is the same as least-squares for normal regression models. </p> <div id="mle-properties" class="section level3"> <h3>MLE properties</h3> <ul> <li>invariant</li> <li>consistent</li> <li>asymptotically unbiased: <span class="math inline">\(E(\beta_{mle}) \overset{p}{\rightarrow} \beta\)</span></li> <li>asymptotically efficient: lowest variance among unbiased estimators</li> <li>asymptotically normally distributed</li> </ul> </div> <div id="mle-parameter-estimation" class="section level3"> <h3>MLE parameter estimation</h3> <ul> <li>single parameter</li> <li>multiple parameters</li> </ul> </div> <div id="mle-hypothesis-testing" class="section level3"> <h3>MLE hypothesis testing</h3> <ul> <li> <span class="math inline">\(H_0: \beta_j=0\)</span> vs. <span class="math inline">\(H_1: \beta_j \ne 0\)</span> <ul> <li>LRT</li> <li>Wald test, score test based on asymptotic distribution of the test statistic, <span class="math inline">\(\chi^2_1\)</span></li> </ul> </li> <li>global test: <span class="math inline">\(H_0: \beta_0=\beta_1=\dots=\beta_j=0\)</span></li> </ul> </div> <div id="mle-confidence-interval" class="section level3"> <h3>MLE confidence interval</h3> <ul> <li>invert a acceptance region of a hypothesis testing</li> <li>so on</li> </ul> </div> <div id="example" class="section level3"> <h3>example</h3> <p> The total July rainfall (in millimetres) at Quilpie, Australia, has been recorded, together with the value of the monthly mean southern oscillation index (soi). we define the response variable y as probability that the rainfall exceeds 10 mm, which we will write as <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span> because this is a <em>Bernoulli distribution</em> with probability <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span> </p> <pre class="r"><code>require(GLMsData)
data(quilpie)
names(quilpie)</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] "Year"   "Rain"   "SOI"    "Phase"  "Exceed" "y"</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>mu <- c(0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8) # Candidate values to test
ll <- rep(0, 5) # A place-holder for the log-likelihood values
for (i in 1:5){
  ll[i] <- sum( dbinom(quilpie$y, size=1, prob=mu[i], log=TRUE))
}
data.frame(Mu=mu, LogLikelihood=ll)</code></pre> <pre><code>##    Mu LogLikelihood
## 1 0.2     -63.69406
## 2 0.4     -48.92742
## 3 0.5     -47.13401
## 4 0.6     -48.11649
## 5 0.8     -60.92148</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>muhat <- mean(quilpie$y)
muhat # mle = sample mean</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 0.5147059</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>boxplot( SOI ~ Exceed, horizontal=TRUE, data=quilpie, las=2,
         xlab="July average SOI", ylab="Rainfall exceeds threshold" )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>plot( jitter(y, 0.15) ~ SOI, data=quilpie, pch=19, axes=FALSE, las=2,
      xlab="July average SOI", ylab="Rainfall exceeds threshold" )
axis(side=1, las=2)
axis(side=2, at=0:1, labels=c("No", "Yes"), las=2); box()</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>cdplot( Exceed ~ SOI, data=quilpie,
        xlab="July average SOI", ylab="Rainfall exceeds threshold" )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>mu0 <- 0.5 # null value
n <- length(quilpie$y)
varmu <- muhat*(1-muhat)/n

# wald test
W <- (muhat - mu0)^2 / varmu
W</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 0.05887446</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># score test
S <- (muhat - mu0)^2 / ( mu0*(1-mu0)/n )
S</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 0.05882353</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># LRT
Lmu0 <- sum( dbinom(quilpie$y, 1, mu0, log=TRUE ) )
Lmuhat <- sum( dbinom(quilpie$y, 1, muhat, log=TRUE ) )
L <- 2*(Lmuhat - Lmu0)
L</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 0.05883201</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>c( Wald=W, score=S, LLR=L)</code></pre> <pre><code>##       Wald      score        LLR 
## 0.05887446 0.05882353 0.05883201</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>P.W <- pchisq(W, df=1, lower.tail=FALSE) # Wald
P.S <- pchisq(S, df=1, lower.tail=FALSE) # Score
P.L <- pchisq(L, df=1, lower.tail=FALSE) # Likelihood ratio
round(c(Wald=P.W, Score=P.S, LLR=P.L), 3 )</code></pre> <pre><code>##  Wald Score   LLR 
## 0.808 0.808 0.808</code></pre> </div> </div> </div> <div id="glm" class="section level1 tabset"> <h1 class="tabset">GLM</h1> <div id="generalized-linear-models-structure" class="section level2"> <h2>generalized linear models: structure</h2> <div id="random-component" class="section level3"> <h3>random component</h3> <p>Specifying the random component by assuming the responses come from the EDM family:</p> <p> <strong>Exponential dispersion model</strong> (EDM) family includes normal and gamma distributions from continuous probability density functions and poisson, binomial, negative binomial distributions from discrete probability mass functions. </p> <p>GLMs are regression models linear in the parameters. GLM = systematic component + random component.</p> <ul> <li> What probability distribution is appropriate? EDMs/Dispersion models <ul> <li>The answer determines the random component of the model.</li> <li>the answer depends on the response data or knowledge of how the variance changes with the mean.</li> </ul> </li> <li> How are the explanatory variables related to the mean of the response? The answer suggests the systematic component of the model. <ul> <li> canonical link function: <span class="math inline">\(g(EY)=\theta=\eta=\beta_0+\sum\beta_jx_j\)</span> where the linear combination of predictors is linked to the mean <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span> through a link function <span class="math inline">\(g(.)\)</span>. <ul> <li> <span class="math inline">\(g(.)\)</span> is monotonic, differentiable function relating fitted <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span> to <span class="math inline">\(\eta\)</span>. </li> <li>this systematic component shows that GLMs are regression models linear in the parameters.</li> </ul> </li> <li>offsets: commonly seen in Poisson GLMs, may be present in other GLMs too</li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p> <strong>EDMs</strong> in <strong>canonical form</strong>: <span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{P}(y|\theta, \phi)=a(y,\phi)\exp\bigg\{ \frac{y\theta-\mathcal{k}(\theta)}{\phi}\bigg\} \]</span> where </p> <ul> <li><span class="math inline">\(\theta\)</span> is the canonical parameter.</li> <li><span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{k}(\theta)\)</span> is a known function, called the <strong>cumulant function</strong>.</li> <li><span class="math inline">\(\phi>0\)</span> is the dispersion parameter.</li> <li> <span class="math inline">\(a(y,\phi)\)</span> is a normalizing function ensuring that <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{P}(y|\theta,\phi)\)</span> is a probability function that it integrates to 1 on <span class="math inline">\((-\infty, \infty)\)</span>. </li> </ul> <p>The mean and variance of the response is can be found by using the cumulant function:</p> <ul> <li> <span class="math inline">\(E[Y]=\mu=\frac{d k(\theta)}{d \theta}\)</span> which is a known function of <span class="math inline">\(\theta\)</span> </li> <li><span class="math inline">\(var[Y]=\phi\frac{d^2 k(\theta)}{d \theta^2}=\phi\frac{d \mu}{d \theta}\)</span></li> <li> define <strong>variance function</strong> as <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu)=\frac{d \mu}{d \theta}\)</span>, then <span class="math inline">\(var[Y]=\phi V(\mu)\)</span> <ul> <li> the variance function <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu)\)</span> <strong>uniquely defines</strong> the distribution within the EDMs </li> <li> <span class="math inline">\(var[Y]=\phi V(\mu)\)</span> specifies: the variance of an EDM depends on the mean, with an exception of normal distribution where <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu)=1\)</span> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p>example as follows:</p> <pre class="r"><code>data(nminer)
breaks <- c(-Inf, 4, 11, 15, 19, Inf) + 0.5 # Break points
Eucs.cut <- cut(nminer$Eucs, breaks )
summary(Eucs.cut)</code></pre> <pre><code>##  (-Inf,4.5]  (4.5,11.5] (11.5,15.5] (15.5,19.5] (19.5, Inf] 
##           9           6           5           6           5</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>mn <- tapply( nminer$Minerab, Eucs.cut, "mean" ) # Mean of each group
vr <- tapply( nminer$Minerab, Eucs.cut, "var" ) # Var of each group
sz <- tapply( nminer$Minerab, Eucs.cut, "length" ) # Num. in each group
cbind("Group size"=sz, "Group mean"=mn, "Group variance"=vr)</code></pre> <pre><code>##             Group size Group mean Group variance
## (-Inf,4.5]           9  0.1111111      0.1111111
## (4.5,11.5]           6  0.5000000      1.5000000
## (11.5,15.5]          5  3.8000000     11.2000000
## (15.5,19.5]          6  4.3333333      7.8666667
## (19.5, Inf]          5  7.0000000     48.5000000</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>plot(jitter(Minerab)~(Eucs), pch=1, las=1, data=nminer, ylim=c(0, 20),
     xlab="Number of eucalypts/2 ha.", ylab="Number of noisy miners")
# Draw the dashed vertical lines
abline(v=breaks, lwd=1, lty=2, col="gray")</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>plot( log( vr ) ~ log ( mn ), pch=19, las=1, cex=0.45*sqrt(sz),
      xlab="Log of means", ylab="Log of variances" )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>hm.lm <- lm( log( vr ) ~ log ( mn ), weights=sz )
coef(hm.lm)</code></pre> <pre><code>## (Intercept)     log(mn) 
##    0.802508    1.295222</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>confint(hm.lm)</code></pre> <pre><code>##                   2.5 %   97.5 %
## (Intercept) 0.007812159 1.597204
## log(mn)     0.821058278 1.769386</code></pre> <p> the slope of the linear regression line (weighted by the number of observations in each group) is <span class="math inline">\(b \approx 1.3\)</span>, suggesting the mean is approximately proportional to the variance. In addition, the estimate of <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is approximately 1 as needed for the Poisson distribution. In other words, <span class="math inline">\(V (\mu) = \mu\)</span> approximately. </p> <p> <strong>EDMs</strong> in <strong>dispersion model form</strong>: instead of writing out the pdf using <span class="math inline">\(\theta\)</span>, try to express it using <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span> since the mean has a clear interpretation as the mean of the distribution. </p> <p><span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{P}(y|\theta, \phi)=b(y,\phi)\exp\bigg\{ -\frac{1}{2 \phi} d(y, \mu) \bigg\} \]</span></p> <p>where:</p> <ul> <li> <span class="math inline">\(d(y, \mu)\)</span> is called <strong>Unit deviance</strong>: <span class="math inline">\(d(y, \mu)=2\{t(y,y)-t(y,\mu)\}, t(y, \mu)=y\theta-k(\theta)\)</span>, which can be interpreted as a type of distance measure between y and <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span>. <ul> <li><span class="math inline">\(t(y,\mu)=y\theta-k(\theta)\)</span></li> </ul> </li> <li> <span class="math inline">\(D(y,\mu)\)</span>, <strong>Deviance function</strong>, its value being <strong>Total deviance</strong>: overall measure of distance between <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i\)</span>. <ul> <li><span class="math inline">\(D(y,\mu)=\sum w_id(y_i, \mu_i)\)</span></li> </ul> </li> <li> <span class="math inline">\(D^*(y, \mu)=D(y,\mu)/\phi\)</span>, <strong>scaled deviance function</strong>, its value being <strong>scaled total deviance</strong> </li> </ul> <p>Common pdfs of the <strong>EDM</strong> family in the <strong>dispersion model form</strong>:</p> <ul> <li> Poisson distribution: <span class="math inline">\(\begin{cases} d(y,\mu)=2\bigg \{ y \log\frac{y}{\mu} -(y-\mu)\bigg \}, \quad y \ne 0 \\ d(0,\mu)=2\mu, \quad y=0 \end{cases}\)</span> </li> <li>Normal distribution: <span class="math inline">\(d(y, \mu)=(y-\mu)^2\)</span></li> <li>Gamma distribution: <span class="math inline">\(d(y,\mu)=2\bigg \{ - \log\frac{y}{\mu} + \frac{(y-\mu)}{\mu}\bigg \}\)</span></li> <li>and more</li> </ul> </div> <div id="systematic-component" class="section level3"> <h3>systematic component</h3> <p> GLMs assume a specific form form of the systematic component to link the mean and linear predictors through a <strong>link function</strong> <span class="math inline">\(g(\cdot)\)</span> so that <span class="math inline">\(g(\mu)=\eta\)</span>. </p> <p><span class="math display">\[ \eta=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_j \]</span></p> <p>the systematic component shows that GLMs are regression models linear in the parameters.</p> <ul> <li> normal: <span class="math inline">\(\theta=\mu\)</span>, the <strong>canonical link function</strong> is <span class="math inline">\(g(\mu)=\mu \Rightarrow \eta=\mu\)</span>, identity link function. </li> <li> Poisson: the <strong>canonical link function</strong> is <span class="math inline">\(g(\mu)=\log \mu\)</span> so that <span class="math inline">\(\log \mu =\eta\)</span> </li> </ul> <p> in some cases, the linear predictor contains a term that requires no estimation, called <strong>offset</strong>. for example, consider modeling the annual number of hospital births in various cities: the annual number of births is discrete, so a Poisson distribution may be suitable; however, the expected annual number of births <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i\)</span> in city <span class="math inline">\(i\)</span> depends on the given population <span class="math inline">\(P_i\)</span> of the city since cities with larger population would be expected to have more births each year, in general; the number of births per unit of populaton, asuming a log-link function can be modelled using the systematic component: <span class="math inline">\(\log(\mu/P)=\eta\)</span>; rearranging gets <span class="math inline">\(\log(\mu)=\log P+\eta\)</span>. The term <span class="math inline">\(\log P\)</span> is normally known and needs not to be estimated, called offset. Offsets commonly appear in Poisson GLMs, but may also appear in any GLMs. </p> <ul> <li> the offset term is commonly a measure of <em>exposure</em>. e.g., the number of cases of a disease recorded in various mines depends on the number of workers, and the number of years each worker has worked in the mine. the exposure would be the number of person-years worked in each mine, which could be an offset term. meaning a mine with many workers employed for many years would be exposed to a greater likelihood of disease than that with only a few less experienced workers. </li> </ul> </div> <div id="glms-defined" class="section level3"> <h3>GLMs defined</h3> <p> Generalized Linear Models is defined as follows: <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} y_i \sim \text{EDM}(\mu_i, \phi/w_i) \\ g(\mu_i)=o_i+\beta_0+\sum\beta_jx_j \end{cases} \]</span> </p> <p>where <span class="math inline">\(o_i\)</span> is th offset terms.</p> </div> </div> <div id="glm-parameter-estimation" class="section level2"> <h2>GLM parameter estimation</h2> <div id="mle-of-regression-coefficients" class="section level3"> <h3>mle of regression coefficients</h3> <p>analytical solution for MLEs for GLMs’ coefficients:</p> <ul> <li>log-likelihood</li> <li>first and second derivative w.r.t. <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j\)</span></li> </ul> <p>computational algorithms for MLE calculation:</p> <ul> <li>Newton-Raphson</li> <li>Fisher Scoring for Computing MLEs</li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code>data("nminer")
nm.m1 <- glm( Minerab ~ Eucs, data=nminer,
              family=poisson(link="log"),
              control=list(trace=TRUE) ) # Shows the deviance each iteration</code></pre> <pre><code>## Deviance = 82.14668 Iterations - 1
## Deviance = 64.49515 Iterations - 2
## Deviance = 63.32603 Iterations - 3
## Deviance = 63.31798 Iterations - 4
## Deviance = 63.31798 Iterations - 5</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>nm.m1</code></pre> <pre><code>## 
## Call:  glm(formula = Minerab ~ Eucs, family = poisson(link = "log"), 
##     data = nminer, control = list(trace = TRUE))
## 
## Coefficients:
## (Intercept)         Eucs  
##     -0.8762       0.1140  
## 
## Degrees of Freedom: 30 Total (i.e. Null);  29 Residual
## Null Deviance:       150.5 
## Residual Deviance: 63.32     AIC: 121.5</code></pre> <ul> <li><code>R</code> uses <strong>total deviance</strong> to declare convergence in probability</li> <li> the <strong>residual deviance</strong>: the minimized total deviance after computing the MLEs for <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j\)</span> and corresponding fitted values of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}, D(y, \hat{\mu})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_id(y_i, \hat{\mu}_i)\)</span>, which is equivalent to RSS that measures the residual variability across n observations for normal linear regression models. </li> </ul> </div> <div id="mle-of-scale-parameter" class="section level3"> <h3>MLE of scale parameter</h3> <ul> <li>analytical solution for linear regression scale param.</li> </ul> <p> consider normal linear regression models, the MLE of <span class="math inline">\(\phi=\sigma^2\)</span> is given as <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{n}\sum w_i(y_i-\hat{\mu}_i)^2\)</span> which is biased. Instead, use sample variance <span class="math inline">\(s^2=\frac{1}{n-p'}\sum w_i(y_i-\hat{\mu}_i)^2\)</span> which is unbiased and used in practice. </p> <ul> <li>generalize to GLMs: modified profile log-likelihood (MPL) estimator</li> </ul> <p>write out the log-likelihood as a function of the scale param,</p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \mathcal{L^{0}}(\phi)=\frac{p'}{2}\log \phi+\mathcal{L}(\hat{\beta}_0, \dots, \hat{\beta}_p;\phi;y) \]</span> compute <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\phi}^{0}\)</span> such that it minimizes the MPL <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{L^{0}}(\phi)\)</span>. the MPL estimator is a consistent and approximately unbiased estimator, even the sample size is small. </p> </div> </div> <div id="glm-inference" class="section level2"> <h2>GLM inference</h2> <p>If <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is <strong>known</strong>:</p> <div id="wald-tests-for-single-coefficient" class="section level3"> <h3>Wald tests for single coefficient</h3> <p>Wald tests are the simplest tests since they depend only on the estimated coefficients and standard errors.</p> <p> The regression coefficients <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\beta}_j\)</span> are asymptotically normally distributed when sample size is reasonably large, which is the basis of Wald tests by Central Limit Thm. </p> <p><span class="math display">\[ H_0: \beta_j=\beta_j^0 \\ \]</span></p> <p> the Wald test statistic is given by <span class="math inline">\(Z=\frac{\hat{\beta}_j-j^0}{\text{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)}\)</span> where <span class="math inline">\(\text{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)=\sqrt{\phi}v_j\)</span>; if <span class="math inline">\(H_0\)</span> is true, Z follows approximately standard normal distribution. </p> </div> <div id="confidence-intervals-for-individual-coefficients" class="section level3"> <h3>confidence intervals for individual coefficients</h3> <p> the <span class="math inline">\(100(1-\alpha)\%\)</span> equal-tail confidence interval for <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j\)</span> when <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is known is given by <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\beta}_j \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)\)</span>. </p> </div> <div id="lrts-for-nested-models" class="section level3"> <h3>LRTs for nested models</h3> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \begin{aligned} &\text{Model A}: g(\hat{\mu}(A))=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1x_1+\cdots+\hat{\beta}_ax_a \\ &\text{Model B}: g(\hat{\mu}(B))=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1x_1+\cdots+\hat{\beta}_ax_a+\cdots+\hat{\beta}_bx_b \\ &H_0: \hat{\beta}_{a+1}x_{a+1}=\cdots=\hat{\beta}_bx_b=0 \end{aligned} \]</span> the LRT statistic is given by: <span class="math inline">\(L=2\{\mathcal{L}(B)-\mathcal{L}(A)\}=\frac{D(y, \hat{\mu}_A)-D(y, \hat{\mu}_B)}{\phi} \sim \chi^2_{p_B-p_A}\)</span>. </p> </div> <div id="analysis-of-deviance-tables-to-compare-nested-models" class="section level3"> <h3>Analysis of deviance tables to compare nested models</h3> </div> <div id="score-tests" class="section level3"> <h3>Score tests</h3> <p> Whereas Wald and likelihood ratio tests (LRTs) are used to test hypotheses about explanatory variables in the current fitted model, score tests enable testing of hypotheses about explanatory variables not (yet) in the current model, but which might be added. </p> </div> <div id="goodness-of-fit-tests" class="section level3"> <h3>goodness-of-fit tests</h3> <p> above tests are used to test for individual coefficient; but here is another question: How many explanatory variables are sufficient? This sort of test is only possible when <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is known, because it requires a known distribution for the residual variability. </p> <p> A goodness-of-fit test compares the current model (Model A say) with an alternative model (Model B) of a particular type where Model B is the largest possible model which can, in principle, be fitted to the data (saturated model). </p> <ul> <li>Deviance goodness-of-fit test</li> <li>Pearson goodness-of-fit test</li> </ul> <p>If <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is <strong>unknown</strong>:</p> </div> <div id="wald-tests-for-single-regression-coefficients" class="section level3"> <h3>Wald tests for single regression coefficients</h3> <p>the Wald test statistic becomes</p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ T=\frac{\hat{\beta}_j-\beta_j^0}{\text{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)} \]</span> where the standard error <span class="math inline">\(\text{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)=sv_j\)</span> needs a suitable estimator <span class="math inline">\(s^2\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span>. the Pearson estimator <span class="math inline">\(s^2=\bar{\phi}\)</span> is used by <code>R</code>. </p> </div> <div id="confidence-intervals-for-individual-coefficients-1" class="section level3"> <h3>confidence intervals for individual coefficients</h3> <p>switch to t-distribution instead of standard normal distribution.</p> </div> <div id="lrts-to-comapare-nested-models-f-tests" class="section level3"> <h3>LRTs to comapare nested models: F-tests</h3> <p> if <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is unknown, an estimate of <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> has be used. An appropriate test statistic for comparing Model A that is nested under Model B is <span class="math inline">\(F=\frac{[D(y,\hat{\mu}_A)-D(y,\hat{\mu}_B)]/(p_B'-p_A')}{s^2}\)</span> where <span class="math inline">\(p_B', p_A'\)</span> indicate number of parameters in Model B, A, respectively. </p> <pre class="r"><code>data(trees)

# F tests for model comparison
tr.m0 <- glm( Volume ~ 1, family=Gamma(link="log"), data=trees)
tr.m1 <- update(tr.m0,.~.+ log(Girth) )
tr.m2 <- update(tr.m1,.~.+ log(Height) )
c( deviance(tr.m0), deviance(tr.m1), deviance(tr.m2) )</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 8.3172012 0.3840839 0.1835153</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>c( df.residual(tr.m0), df.residual(tr.m1), df.residual(tr.m2) )</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 30 29 28</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>dev1 <- deviance(tr.m0) - deviance(tr.m1)
dev2 <- deviance(tr.m1) - deviance(tr.m2)
df1 <- df.residual(tr.m0) - df.residual(tr.m1)
df2 <- df.residual(tr.m1) - df.residual(tr.m2)
c( dev1, dev2)</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 7.9331173 0.2005686</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>c( df1, df2)</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 1 1</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>phi.meandev <- deviance(tr.m2) / df.residual(tr.m2) # Mean dev. estimate
phi.Pearson <- summary(tr.m2)$dispersion # Pearson estimate
c("Mean deviance" = phi.meandev, "Pearson" = phi.Pearson )</code></pre> <pre><code>## Mean deviance       Pearson 
##   0.006554117   0.006427286</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>F.Pearson <- c( dev1/df1, dev2/df2 ) / phi.Pearson # calculate obs.
F.meandev <- c( dev1/df1, dev2/df2 ) / phi.meandev
P.Pearson <- pf( F.Pearson, df1, df.residual(tr.m2), lower.tail=FALSE ) # calculate p-value
P.meandev <- pf( F.meandev, df2, df.residual(tr.m2), lower.tail=FALSE )
tab <- data.frame(F.Pearson, P.Pearson, F.meandev, P.meandev)
rownames(tab) <- c("Girth","Height")
print(tab, digits=3)</code></pre> <pre><code>##        F.Pearson P.Pearson F.meandev P.meandev
## Girth     1234.3  1.05e-24    1210.4  1.38e-24
## Height      31.2  5.60e-06      30.6  6.50e-06</code></pre> </div> <div id="anaysis-of-deviance-tables-to-compare-nested-models" class="section level3"> <h3>anaysis of deviance tables to compare nested models</h3> <p>to compare a series of GLMs, an analysis of deviance table is used:</p> <pre class="r"><code>anova(tr.m2, test="F")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: Gamma, link: log
## 
## Response: Volume
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##             Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev        F    Pr(>F)    
## NULL                           30     8.3172                       
## log(Girth)   1   7.9331        29     0.3841 1234.287 < 2.2e-16 ***
## log(Height)  1   0.2006        28     0.1835   31.206 5.604e-06 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> </div> </div> <div id="glm-comparison" class="section level2"> <h2>GLM Comparison</h2> <ul> <li> Nested models <ul> <li>LRT</li> <li>Drop-in-Deviance test</li> </ul> </li> <li> Non-nested models <ul> <li> if <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is unknown <ul> <li>AIC<span class="math inline">\(=-2\times \mathcal{L}(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\phi};y)+2(p'+1)\)</span></li> <li>BIC<span class="math inline">\(=-2\times \mathcal{L}(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\phi};y)+(\log n)(p'+1)\)</span></li> <li><span class="math inline">\(\hat{\phi}\)</span> is the MLE of <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span></li> <li>smaller values of the AIC/BIC (closer to <span class="math inline">\(-\infty\)</span>) represent better models.</li> </ul> </li> <li> if <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is known <ul> <li>AIC<span class="math inline">\(=-2\times \mathcal{L}(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\phi};y)+2p'\)</span></li> <li>BIC<span class="math inline">\(=-2\times \mathcal{L}(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\phi};y)+(\log n)p'\)</span></li> </ul> </li> </ul> </li> <li> Automated model selection <ul> <li>forward/backward/mixed step-wise variable selection</li> <li> the same automatic procedures used in normal linear regression case can also be used for GLMs: <code>drop1()</code>, <code>add1()</code>, <code>step()</code> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code># information criteria
tr.aic1 <- glm( Volume ~ offset(2*log(Girth)) + log(Height),
                family=Gamma(link="log"), data=trees)
tr.aic2 <- glm( Volume ~ log(Girth) + offset(log(Height)),
                family=Gamma(link="log"), data=trees)
c(AIC(tr.aic1), AIC(tr.aic2))</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1] 137.9780 138.3677</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># automated selection
min.model <- glm( Volume~1, data=trees, family=Gamma(link="log"))
max.model <- glm( Volume~log(Girth) + log(Height), data=trees, family=Gamma(link="log"))
m.b <- step(min.model, scope=list(lower=min.model, upper=max.model), direction="both")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Start:  AIC=255.48
## Volume ~ 1
## 
##               Df Deviance    AIC
## + log(Girth)   1   0.3841 230.75
## + log(Height)  1   4.7827 245.57
## <none>             8.3172 255.48
## 
## Step:  AIC=160.83
## Volume ~ log(Girth)
## 
##               Df Deviance    AIC
## + log(Height)  1   0.1835 147.82
## <none>             0.3841 160.83
## - log(Girth)   1   8.3172 752.55
## 
## Step:  AIC=139.9
## Volume ~ log(Girth) + log(Height)
## 
##               Df Deviance    AIC
## <none>             0.1835 139.90
## - log(Height)  1   0.3841 169.11
## - log(Girth)   1   4.7827 853.48</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>m.a <- step(min.model, scope=list(lower=min.model, upper=max.model), direction="backward")</code></pre> <pre><code>## Start:  AIC=255.48
## Volume ~ 1</code></pre> </div> <div id="glm-diagnostics" class="section level2"> <h2>GLM Diagnostics</h2> <div id="assumptions-of-glms" class="section level3"> <h3>Assumptions of GLMs</h3> <p> the assumptions are never exactly true. it is important to be aware of that the sensitivity of the conclusions to the deviations from the assumptions. </p> <ul> <li> Lack of outliers: All responses were generated from the same process, so that the same model is appropriate for all the observations. </li> <li>Link function: The correct link function g() is used.</li> <li> Linearity: All important explanatory variables are included, and each explanatory variable is included in the linear predictor on the correct scale. </li> <li>Variance function: The correct variance function <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu_i)\)</span> is used.</li> <li>Dispersion parameter: The dispersion parameter <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is constant.</li> <li>Independence: The responses <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span> are independent of each other.</li> <li>Distribution: The responses <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span> come from the specified EDM.</li> </ul> </div> <div id="residuals-for-glms" class="section level3"> <h3>residuals for GLMs</h3> <p> the distances <span class="math inline">\(y_i-\hat{\mu}_i\)</span> are called <strong>response residuals</strong>, and are the basis for residuals in linear regression. The <strong>response residuals</strong> are inadequate for assessing a fitted GLM since for GLMs within EDMs, the <strong>variance depends on the mean</strong> through the variance function <span class="math inline">\(V(\mu_i)\)</span>. </p> <p> the case can be where the distances <span class="math inline">\(y_i-\hat{\mu}_i\)</span> are the same for two responses, but one of them is extreme while the other is not. ideally, we want residuals to be like the residuals from linear regression models where they are normally distributed with mean 0 and a constant variance. </p> <ul> <li>Pearson residuals: <span class="math inline">\(r_p=\frac{y-\hat{\mu}}{\sqrt{V(\hat{\mu})/w}}\)</span></li> <li> Deviance residuals: <span class="math inline">\(r_D=\text{sign}(y-\hat{\mu})\sqrt{wd(y, \hat{\mu})}\)</span>, <code>residual(fit)</code> computes deviance residuals by default. </li> <li> Quantile residuals: when the guidelines for GLMs asymptotics not met and the Pearson and deviance residual clearly cannot be normally distributed. try <code>qresid(fit)</code> from <code>statmod</code> package. <ul> <li>Quantile residuals are especially encouraged for discrete EDMs</li> <li>standardized or studentized residual are encouraged as they have more constant variance.</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="checking-glm-assumptions" class="section level3"> <h3>checking GLM assumptions</h3> <ul> <li> independence: independence of the responses is the <strong>most important assumption</strong>. <ul> <li>plot residuals against lagged residuals</li> </ul> </li> <li> plot to check <strong>systematic component</strong> <ul> <li> plot standardized/quantile residuals against <strong>fitted values</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}_i\)</span> <ul> <li> to further check on <strong>link function</strong>, plot working responses against <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\eta}i\)</span>; if any curvature, another link function is needed. </li> </ul> </li> <li> plot standardized/quantile residuals against <strong>predictor</strong> <span class="math inline">\(x_j\)</span> <ul> <li> to determine if predictor is included on the correct scale, use <em>partial residuals</em>: <code>resid(fit, type="partial")</code> </li> <li>Two features to check for the residuals plots:<br/></li> <li> <em>Trends</em>: Any trends appearing in these plots indicate that the systematic component can be improved. <ul> <li> This could mean changing the link function, adding extra explanatory variables, or transforming the explanatory variables. </li> </ul> </li> <li> <em>Constant variation</em>: If the random component is correct (that is, the correct EDM is used), the variance of the points is approximately constant. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code>data(trees)
cherry.m1 <- glm( Volume ~ log(Girth) + log(Height),
                  family=Gamma(link=log), data=trees)

scatter.smooth( rstandard(cherry.m1) ~ log(fitted(cherry.m1)), las=1,
                ylab="Standardized deviance residual", xlab="log(Fitted values)" )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>scatter.smooth( rstandard(cherry.m1) ~ log(trees$Girth), las=1,
                ylab="Standardized deviance residual", xlab="log(Girth)" )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>scatter.smooth( rstandard(cherry.m1) ~ log(trees$Height), las=1,
                ylab="Standardized deviance residual", xlab="log(Height)" )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code># working responses vs. eta to check on systematic component
z <- resid(cherry.m1, type="working") + cherry.m1$linear.predictor
plot( z ~ cherry.m1$linear.predictor, las=1, 
      xlab="Working responses, z", 
      ylab="Linear predictor")
abline(a=0, b=1)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code># partial residuals vs predictor for predictor scale 
termplot(cherry.m1, partial.resid=TRUE, las=1)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <p> The plot of <span class="math inline">\(z_i\)</span> against <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\eta}_i\)</span> is also approximately linear suggesting a suitable link function. The line shown on each <code>termplot()</code> represents is the ideal relationship, suggesting predictors are included on the suitable scale. </p> <ul> <li> plot to check <strong>random component</strong> <ul> <li> plot to check random component <ul> <li>Q-Q plots can be used to determine if the choice of distribution is appropriate.</li> <li>quantile residuals are used since thet have an exact normal dist.</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code>qr.cherry <- qresid( cherry.m1 ) # extract quantile residuals
qqnorm( qr.cherry, las=1 ); qqline( qr.cherry)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <ul> <li> outliers & influential obs <ul> <li>outliers: obs. inconsistent with the rest of data</li> <li> influential obs: obs. that substantially change the fitted model when removed <ul> <li>influential observations are outliers with high leverage.</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <pre class="r"><code># outliers by studentized residual
rs <- cbind( rD=resid(cherry.m1), 
             "r'D"=rstandard(cherry.m1),
             "r''"=rstudent(cherry.m1), 
             rQ=qresid(cherry.m1))

apply( abs(rs), 2, max) # The maximum absolute for each residual</code></pre> <pre><code>##       rD      r'D      r''       rQ 
## 0.166763 2.197761 2.329122 2.053011</code></pre> <p> Since <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is small in this case, the saddlepoint approximation is suitable, and the quantile, standardized and Studentized residuals are very similar. No large residuals exist. </p> <p> An approximation to Cook’s distance for GLMs is D as computed by the function <code>cooks.distance()</code> in <code>R</code>, where the Pearson estimator <span class="math inline">\(\bar{\phi}\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> is used if it is unknown. </p> <pre class="r"><code>im <- influence.measures(cherry.m1)

im$infmat <- round(im$infmat, 3 )
head(im$infmat)</code></pre> <pre><code>##   dfb.1_ dfb.l(G) dfb.l(H)  dffit cov.r cook.d   hat
## 1  0.015   -0.083    0.005  0.107 1.305  0.004 0.151
## 2  0.120   -0.082   -0.090  0.197 1.311  0.014 0.167
## 3  0.065   -0.021   -0.054  0.087 1.385  0.003 0.198
## 4 -0.011    0.021    0.004 -0.041 1.181  0.001 0.059
## 5  0.145    0.171   -0.170 -0.228 1.218  0.018 0.121
## 6  0.186    0.191   -0.212 -0.261 1.261  0.023 0.152</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>head(im$is.inf)</code></pre> <pre><code>##   dfb.1_ dfb.l(G) dfb.l(H) dffit cov.r cook.d   hat
## 1  FALSE    FALSE    FALSE FALSE FALSE  FALSE FALSE
## 2  FALSE    FALSE    FALSE FALSE FALSE  FALSE FALSE
## 3  FALSE    FALSE    FALSE FALSE  TRUE  FALSE FALSE
## 4  FALSE    FALSE    FALSE FALSE FALSE  FALSE FALSE
## 5  FALSE    FALSE    FALSE FALSE FALSE  FALSE FALSE
## 6  FALSE    FALSE    FALSE FALSE FALSE  FALSE FALSE</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>colSums( im$is.inf )</code></pre> <pre><code>##   dfb.1_ dfb.l(G) dfb.l(H)    dffit    cov.r   cook.d      hat 
##        0        0        0        0        3        0        0</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># plot out im
cherry.cd <- cooks.distance( cherry.m1)
plot( cherry.cd, type="h", ylab="Cook's distance", las=1)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>plot( dffits(cherry.m1), type="h", las=1, ylab="DFFITS")</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>infl <- which.max(cherry.cd) # The Observation number of largest D
infl # Which observation?</code></pre> <pre><code>## 18 
## 18</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code>cherry.cd[infl] # The value of D for that observation</code></pre> <pre><code>##        18 
## 0.2067211</code></pre> <p> Three observations are identified as influential, but only by cr. Since none of the other measures identify these observations as influential, we should not be too concerned. </p> <p> The value of Cook’s distance for Observation 18 is much larger than any others, but the observation is not identified as significantly influential. </p> </div> </div> <div id="remedy" class="section level2"> <h2>Remedy</h2> <div id="quasi-likelihood" class="section level3"> <h3>quasi-likelihood</h3> <p> when there is no EDM for a given mean-variance relationship, quasi-likelihood provides a way to conduct inference. by <code>family=quasipoisson()</code>, etc. </p> </div> </div> <div id="example-1" class="section level2"> <h2>example</h2> <p>The GLM fitted to model the number of noisy miners from the number of eucalypt trees is:</p> <pre class="r"><code>data(nminer)
nm.m1 <- glm( Minerab ~ Eucs, data=nminer, family=poisson)
printCoefmat(coef(summary(nm.m1)))</code></pre> <pre><code>##              Estimate Std. Error z value  Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept) -0.876211   0.282793 -3.0984  0.001946 ** 
## Eucs         0.113981   0.012431  9.1691 < 2.2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1</code></pre> <pre class="r"><code># systematic & random components, outliers
qr <- qresid( nm.m1 )  # To find randomized quantile residuals
qqnorm(qr, las=1)
qqline(qr)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>plot( qr ~ sqrt(fitted(nm.m1)), las=1 )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code># influential points
plot( cooks.distance(nm.m1), type="h", las=1 )</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>plot( hatvalues(nm.m1), type="h", las=1)</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672" style="display: block; margin: auto"/> </p> <pre class="r"><code>maxhat <- which.max( hatvalues(nm.m1) ) # Largest leverage
maxqr <- which.max( abs(qr) ) # Largest abs. residual
maxinfl <- which.max( cooks.distance(nm.m1)) # Most influential
c( MaxLeverage=maxhat, MaxResid=maxqr, MaxInfluence=maxinfl)</code></pre> <pre><code>##  MaxLeverage.11        MaxResid MaxInfluence.17

## 17</code></pre> <p>Only Observation 17 is influential: Observation 17 has a reasonably large residual and leverage, and so it is influential.</p> <p>Observe the changes in the regression coefficients after omitting obs.17:</p> <pre class="r"><code>nm.m2 <- glm( Minerab ~ Eucs,

              subset=(-maxinfl)) # A negative index removes the obs.

      /**

      (function ($) {

            var selector = hash ? 'a[href="' + hash + '"]' : "li.active > a";

            }

          });

      window.buildTabsets = function (tocID) {

        function buildTabset(tabset) {
          // check for fade and pills options
          var fade = tabset.hasClass("tabset-fade");
          var pills = tabset.hasClass("tabset-pills");
          var navClass = pills ? "nav-pills" : "nav-tabs";

          // determine the heading level of the tabset and tabs
          var match = tabset.attr("class").match(/level(\d) /);

          var tabLevel = tabsetLevel + 1;

          // find all subheadings immediately below
          var tabs = tabset.find("div.section.level" + tabLevel);
          if (!tabs.length) return;

          // create tablist and tab-content elements
          var tabList = $('<ul class="nav ' + navClass + '" role="tablist"></ul>');
          $(tabs[0]).before(tabList);
          var tabContent = $('<div class="tab-content"></div>');
          $(tabs[0]).before(tabContent);

          // build the tabset
          var activeTab = 0;

            var tab = $(tabs[i]);

            var id = tab.attr("id");

            if (tab.hasClass("active")) activeTab = i;

            id = id.replace(/[.\/?&!#<>]/g, "").replace(/\s/g, "_");
            tab.attr("id", id);

            // get the heading element within it, grab it's text, then remove it
            var heading = tab.find("h" + tabLevel + ":first");
            var headingText = heading.html();
            heading.remove();

            var a = $('<a role="tab" data-toggle="tab">' + headingText + "</a>");
            a.attr("href", "#" + id);
            a.attr("aria-controls", id);
            var li = $('<li role="presentation"></li>');
            li.append(a);
            tabList.append(li);

            // set it's attributes
            tab.attr("role", "tabpanel");
            tab.addClass("tab-pane");
            tab.addClass("tabbed-pane");
            if (fade) tab.addClass("fade");

            // move it into the tab content div
            tab.detach().appendTo(tabContent);
          });

        }

        var tabsets = $("div.section.tabset");
        tabsets.each(function (i) {

</div> <div class="toc-content col-xs-12 col-sm-8 col-md-9"> <div id="header"> <h1 class="title toc-ignore">Regression Models</h1> <h4 class="author">Tuo Liu</h4> <h4 class="date">2024-06-21</h4> </div> <div id="statistical-models" class="section level1 tabset"> <h1 class="tabset">statistical models</h1> <div id="notation-and-foundation" class="section level2"> <h2>notation and foundation</h2> <p> All models are wrong, but some are useful: models are not an exact representation of reality; models are useful approximations for representing the necessary detail for the purpose at hand. </p> </div> <div id="statistical-modelsrandomsystematic-components" class="section level2"> <h2>statistical models=random+systematic components</h2> <p> consider a lung capacity experiment where lung capacity data were collected along with age, gender and smoking status. At any combination of height, age, and smoking status, many different values of lung capacity could be recorded, and so produce a distribution of recorded lung capacity values. A model for this distribution of values is called the <strong>random component</strong> of the statistical model. At a given combination of height, age, gender and smoking status, the distribution of lung capacity values has a mean. The mathematical relationshio between the mean and given values of the predictors is called the <strong>systematic component</strong> of the statistical model. </p> <p> a ststistical model consists of a random component and a systematic component to explain these two features of real data. A statistical model is to mathematically represent both the systematic and random components of data. </p> <p>many systematic components for the lung capacity data are possible. One simple systematic component is</p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \mu_i = \beta_0+\beta_1 x_{1i}+\beta_2 x_{2i}+\dots+\beta_px_{pi} \]</span> for observation i, where <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i\)</span> is the expected value of <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span>, so that <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i=E[y_i]\)</span> for <span class="math inline">\(i=1,2,\dots, n\)</span>. The <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j\)</span> are unknown regression parameters. Plotting y against exploratory variables indicates that this is a poor systematic component. the random component about this systematic components may take many forms. for example, <span class="math inline">\(var[y_i]=\sigma^2\)</span> assumes that the variance of the responses <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span> is constant about <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i\)</span> without assuming the distribution of the responses. A popular assumption is to assume the responses are normally distributed around <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span>, written as <span class="math inline">\(y_i \sim N(\mu_i, \sigma^2)\)</span>. Both assumptions on constant variance are likely to be poor as the variation in the observed lung capacity increases for larger values of FEV. </p> <p> Combining the random and systematic component, a possible linear regression model for modelling lung capacity data is <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} var[y_i]=\sigma^2 \\ \mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{1i}+\dots+\beta_px_{pi} \end{cases} \]</span> </p> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> </div> <div id="regression-models" class="section level2"> <h2>regression models</h2> <p> generally, a regression model assumes that the mean response <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i\)</span> for observation i depends on the p predictors <span class="math inline">\(x_{1i}, \dots, x_{pi}\)</span> via some general function <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> through a number of regression parameters <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j\)</span>: <span class="math display">\[ E[y_i]=\mu_i=f(x_{1i}, \dots, x_{pi};\beta_0, \dots, \beta_p) \]</span> commonly, the parameters <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j\)</span> are assumed to combine the effects of predictors linearly, thus the systematic component takes a more specific form </p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \mu_i=f(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{1i}+\dots+\beta_px_{pi}) \]</span> so called linear regression models. There are two special cases of regression models linear in the parameters well studies: </p> <ul> <li> linear regression models: the systematic component of a linear regression model assumes the form <span class="math inline">\(E[y_i]=\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{1i}+\dots+\beta_px_{pi}\)</span> while the randomness is assumed to be constant <span class="math inline">\(\sigma^2\)</span> about <span class="math inline">\(\mu_i\)</span> </li> <li> generalized linear models: the systematic component of a generalized linear model assumes the form <span class="math inline">\(g(\mu_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{1i}+\dots+\beta_px_{pi}\)</span> where <span class="math inline">\(g(\cdot)\)</span> is monotonic, differentiable function, called <strong>link function</strong>. the randomness is explained by assuming y comes from a specific family of pdf. </li> </ul> </div> <div id="purpose-of-a-statistical-model-prediction-vs-interpretation" class="section level2"> <h2>purpose of a statistical model: prediction vs interpretation</h2> <p> the role of a statistical model is to accurately represent the important systematic and random features of the data. The purpose of developing statistical models can be two-fold: </p> <ul> <li>prediction: to provide accurate predictions from new or future data</li> <li>understanding and interpretation: to understand how variable relate to each other</li> </ul> </div> <div id="accuracy-vs-parsimony" class="section level2"> <h2>accuracy vs parsimony</h2> <p>in general, an adequate statistical model balances two criteria:</p> <ul> <li>accuracy: the model should accurately describe both the systematic and random components</li> <li> parsimony: the model should be as simple as possible for better understanding and interpretability <ul> <li>overfitting; follow details, fit the data extremely well but poor generalization performance for future data</li> <li>underfitting: model is too simple to capture data features</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="experiemnts-vs-observational-studies" class="section level2"> <h2>experiemnts vs observational studies</h2> <p> “All models must be used and understood within limitations imposed by how the data were collected.” the method of data collection affects the conclusions that can be drawn from the analysis. </p> <p> in an observational study, researchers may use elaborate equipment to collect physical measures or ask well designed questions, but do not control the process being observed. Observational studies generally only permit conclusions about associations, not a cause-and-effect. </p> <p> in a designed experiment, researchers fo intervene to control the values of the exploratory variables that appear in the data such that they are able to determine which experimental condition is applied to each subject. A well-designed randomized experiment allows for cause-and-effect relationships. </p> <p> statistical models treat experimental and observational studies the same way, and the statistical conclusions are similar. However, the scientific conclusions from experiments are usually much stronger. The best we can do in an observational study is to collect as many extraneous variables that are likely to affect the response, so that as many uncontrolled effects can be adjusted for. </p> </div> </div> <div id="linear-regression-models" class="section level1 tabset"> <h1 class="tabset">linear regression models</h1> <div id="model-definition" class="section level2"> <h2>model definition</h2> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \begin{cases} var[y_i]=\sigma^2/w_i \\ \mu_i=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ji} \end{cases} \]</span> </p> <ul> <li>simple linear regression model: when <span class="math inline">\(p'=2\)</span></li> <li>ordinary linear regression model: when all prior weights <span class="math inline">\(w_i=1\)</span></li> <li>weighted linear regression model: when prior weights are not equal</li> <li>multiple linear regression model</li> </ul> <p>necessary assumptions for establishing linear regression models are:</p> <ul> <li>suitability: the same regression model is appropriate for all observations [outliers]</li> <li>linearity: the true relationship between <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span> and each continuous predictor is linear</li> <li>constant variance</li> <li>independence: the responses y are independent of each other</li> </ul> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> <pre><code>## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Weight ~ Age, data = gestation, weights = Births)

To summarize the deviations, square them to avoid negative quantities then sum them: </p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ S(\beta_0, \beta_1)=\sum_{i}^{n}w_ie_i^2=\sum_{i}^{n}w_i(y_i-\mu_i)^2=\sum_{i}^{n}w_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2 \]</span> The non-negative weights <span class="math inline">\(w_i\)</span> may be used to weight observations according to their precision; S summarizes how far the fitted line deviates from the observations. </p> <p>intuitively, the least-squares estimators of <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j\)</span> can be found by minimizing S.</p> <p> using calculus, solving <span class="math display">\[ \frac{\partial S}{\partial \beta_0}=0 \Rightarrow \hat{\beta_0}; \frac{\partial S}{\partial \beta_1}=0 \Rightarrow \hat{\beta_1} \]</span> least-squares estimators are unbiased; the fitted means are given by <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}_i=\hat{\beta_0}+\hat{\beta_1}x_i\)</span> for <span class="math inline">\(i=1,\dots,n\)</span>. </p> <p>the minimized value of S, evaluated at the least-squares estimates, is called <strong>residual sum-of-squares (RSS)</strong>:</p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ \text{RSS}=\sum_{i}^{n}w_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2 \bigg |_{\hat{\beta_0}, \hat{\beta_1}}=\sum_{i}^{n}w_i(y_i-\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1x_i)^2 \]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(r_i=y_i-\hat{\mu}_i\)</span> is called the <strong>raw residuals</strong>. </p> <ul> <li> <p> estimating <strong>variance</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\sigma^2\)</span> by <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{RSS}{n}\)</span> by definition of variance leads to a biased estimator; <span class="math inline">\(\frac{RSS}{n-2}\)</span> is unbiased and used in practice by considering that RSS is based on loss of two degrees of freedom. more generally, for multiple linear regression, <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{RSS}{n-p}\)</span>. </p> </li> <li> <p> standard error is used in statistics to denote the standard deviation of an estimated quantity. <span class="math inline">\(se(\hat{\beta}_0), se(\hat{\beta}_1)\)</span>. </p> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="model-comparison" class="section level2"> <h2>model comparison</h2> <div id="nested-anova" class="section level3"> <h3>nested: anova</h3> <pre><code>##   ModelA   ModelB

This suggests that the model is poor. </p> </li> <li> <p>residuals vs. <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}\)</span>: constant variance</p> </li> </ul> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> - Q-Q plot for normality <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> </div> </div> <div id="remedies" class="section level2"> <h2>remedies</h2> <div id="transforming-y" class="section level3"> <h3>transforming y</h3> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> <p> <strong>Box-Cox transformation</strong> finds the optimal <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> to achieve linearity, normality and constant variance simultaneously. </p> <pre><code>## Loading required package: MASS</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> </div> <div id="transforming-covariates" class="section level3"> <h3>transforming covariates</h3> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> </div> <div id="polynomial-trend" class="section level3"> <h3>polynomial trend</h3> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> <pre><code>##             (Intercept)       Temp  I(Temp^2)

For this reason, natural smoothing splines are a good practical choice in most cases for fitting data-driven curves. </p> <pre><code>## Loading required package: splines</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1]    4.0000 -117.1234</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1]    4.0000 -119.2705</code></pre> <pre><code>## [1]    4.0000 -117.1234</code></pre> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> <pre><code>## [[1]]

Sometimes, however, they do remain. </p> <ul> <li> first step: identify thier cause <ul> <li>by mistake: mis-recorded observations, then correct or discard the observation.</li> <li>from a different population: dsicarded.</li> <li> no known reason for why it may be an outlier: An outlier that is not a mistake suggests that a different or more complex model may be necessary. One strategy to evaluate the influence of the outlier is to fit the model to the data with and without the outlier. If the two models are materially different, perhaps other types of models should be considered. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="collinearity" class="section level3"> <h3>collinearity</h3> <p> Collinearity means that different combinations of the covariates may lead to nearly the same fitted values. Collinearity is therefore mainly a problem for interpretation rather than prediction. </p> <p> A special case of collinearity occurs when a covariate and a power of the covariate are included in the same model. Using orthogonal polynomials or regression splines avoids this problem. </p> <p>If collinearity is detected or suspected, remedies include:</p> <ul> <li>Omitting some explanatory variables</li> <li>Combine explanatory variables in the model provided the combination makes sense.</li> <li>Use special methods, such as ridge, lasso regression</li> </ul> <p> <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="672"/> </p> <pre><code>##               Cases  Eligible   OpRooms MainHours

      /**
       * jQuery Plugin: Sticky Tabs
       *
       * @author Aidan Lister <aidan@php.net>
       * adapted by Ruben Arslan to activate parent tabs too
       * http://www.aidanlister.com/2014/03/persisting-the-tab-state-in-bootstrap/
       */
      (function ($) {
        "use strict";
        $.fn.rmarkdownStickyTabs = function () {
          var context = this;
          // Show the tab corresponding with the hash in the URL, or the first tab
          var showStuffFromHash = function () {
            var hash = window.location.hash;
            var selector = hash ? 'a[href="' + hash + '"]' : "li.active > a";
            var $selector = $(selector, context);
            if ($selector.data("toggle") === "tab") {
              $selector.tab("show");
              // walk up the ancestors of this element, show any hidden tabs
              $selector.parents(".section.tabset").each(function (i, elm) {
                var link = $('a[href="#' + $(elm).attr("id") + '"]');
                if (link.data("toggle") === "tab") {
                  link.tab("show");
                }
              });
            }
          };

          // Set the correct tab when the page loads
          showStuffFromHash(context);

          // Set the correct tab when a user uses their back/forward button
          $(window).on("hashchange", function () {
            showStuffFromHash(context);
          });

          // Change the URL when tabs are clicked
          $("a", context).on("click", function (e) {
            history.pushState(null, null, this.href);
            showStuffFromHash(context);
          });

          return this;
        };
      })(jQuery);

      window.buildTabsets = function (tocID) {
        // build a tabset from a section div with the .tabset class
        function buildTabset(tabset) {
          // check for fade and pills options
          var fade = tabset.hasClass("tabset-fade");
          var pills = tabset.hasClass("tabset-pills");
          var navClass = pills ? "nav-pills" : "nav-tabs";

          // determine the heading level of the tabset and tabs
          var match = tabset.attr("class").match(/level(\d) /);
          if (match === null) return;
          var tabsetLevel = Number(match[1]);
          var tabLevel = tabsetLevel + 1;

          // find all subheadings immediately below
          var tabs = tabset.find("div.section.level" + tabLevel);
          if (!tabs.length) return;

          // create tablist and tab-content elements
          var tabList = $('<ul class="nav ' + navClass + '" role="tablist"></ul>');
          $(tabs[0]).before(tabList);
          var tabContent = $('<div class="tab-content"></div>');
          $(tabs[0]).before(tabContent);

          // build the tabset
          var activeTab = 0;
          tabs.each(function (i) {
            // get the tab div
            var tab = $(tabs[i]);

            // get the id then sanitize it for use with bootstrap tabs
            var id = tab.attr("id");

            // see if this is marked as the active tab
            if (tab.hasClass("active")) activeTab = i;

            // remove any table of contents entries associated with
            // this ID (since we'll be removing the heading element)
            $("div#" + tocID + " li a[href='#" + id + "']")
              .parent()
              .remove();

            // sanitize the id for use with bootstrap tabs
            id = id.replace(/[.\/?&!#<>]/g, "").replace(/\s/g, "_");
            tab.attr("id", id);

            // get the heading element within it, grab it's text, then remove it
            var heading = tab.find("h" + tabLevel + ":first");
            var headingText = heading.html();
            heading.remove();

            // build and append the tab list item
            var a = $('<a role="tab" data-toggle="tab">' + headingText + "</a>");
            a.attr("href", "#" + id);
            a.attr("aria-controls", id);
            var li = $('<li role="presentation"></li>');
            li.append(a);
            tabList.append(li);

            // set it's attributes
            tab.attr("role", "tabpanel");
            tab.addClass("tab-pane");
            tab.addClass("tabbed-pane");
            if (fade) tab.addClass("fade");

            // move it into the tab content div
            tab.detach().appendTo(tabContent);
          });

          // set active tab
          $(tabList.children("li")[activeTab]).addClass("active");
          var active = $(tabContent.children("div.section")[activeTab]);
          active.addClass("active");
          if (fade) active.addClass("in");

          if (tabset.hasClass("tabset-sticky")) tabset.rmarkdownStickyTabs();
        }

        // convert section divs with the .tabset class to tabsets
        var tabsets = $("div.section.tabset");
        tabsets.each(function (i) {
          buildTabset($(tabsets[i]));
        });
      };

p-valuesand false discovery rates</a> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="statistical-learning" class="section level1"> <h1>Statistical-Learning</h1> <div id="overview" class="section level2"> <h2>Overview</h2> <ul> <li> <strong>statistical learning</strong> <span class="citation">(Gareth James 2021)</span> refers to a vast set of tools for understanding data. These tools can be classified as: <ul> <li>supervised: building a statistical model for predicting, or estimating, an <em>output</em> based on one or more inputs.</li> <li>unsupervised: there are inputs but no supervising output; learn relationships and structure from such data.</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="history" class="section level2"> <h2>History</h2> <ul> <li>19th century-<em>least squares</em> method was developed</li> <li>1936-<em>linear discriminant analysis</em> to predict qualitative values</li> <li>1940s-logistic regression</li> <li> 1970s-generalized linear model was developed to describe an entire class of statistical learning methods that include both linear and logistic regression as special cases. </li> <li> 1980s-<em>classification</em> and <em>regression trees</em> were developed, followed by <em>generalized additive models</em>. <em>Neural networks</em> gained popularity. </li> <li>1990s-<em>support vector machines</em> arose.</li> </ul> </div> <div id="organization" class="section level2"> <h2>organization</h2> <ul> <li>chap 2: terminology and concepts behind statistical learning + K-means classifier</li> <li>chap 3: linear regression</li> <li>chap 4: logistic regression + linear discriminant analysis</li> <li>chap 5: cross-validation + bootstrap: choosing the best method</li> <li>chap 6: improvement on classical linear regression - stepwise selection, ridge regression, principal components regression, lasso</li> <li>chap 7: non-linear methods work well with one input variable, non-linear additive methods for more than one input variables</li> <li>chap 8: tree-based methods, including bagging, boosting, random forests</li> <li>chap 9: support vector machines that performs both linear and non-linear classification</li> <li>chap 10: deep learning that performs non-linear regression and classification</li> <li> chap 11: survival analysis, a regression approach specialized to the setting in whcih the output is <em>censored</em>, i.e., not fully observed. </li> <li>chap 12: unsupervised settings, principal component analysis, K-means clustering, hierarchical clustering</li> <li>chap 13: multiple hypothesis testing</li> </ul> </div> <div id="chap-2.-statistical-learning" class="section level2"> <h2>chap 2. statistical learning</h2> <p> our goal is to develop an accurate model that can be used to predict sales on the basis of the three media budgets. More generally, suppose that we observe a quantitative response <span class="math inline">\(Y\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> different predictors, <span class="math inline">\(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_p\)</span>. We assume that there is some relationship between Y and <span class="math inline">\(X=(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_p)\)</span>, wchih can be written in the very general form: <span class="math display">\[ Y=f(X)+\epsilon \]</span> Here <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> is some fixed but unknown function of <span class="math inline">\(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_p\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\epsilon\)</span> is a random error term, which is independent of X and had mean zero. In this formulation, <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> represents the systematic information that X provides about Y. </p> <p>In essence, statistical learning refers to a set of approaches for estimating <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span>.</p> <div id="whats-statistical-learning" class="section level3"> <h3>What’s statistical learning?</h3> <div id="why-estimate-f" class="section level4"> <h4>Why estimate f?</h4> <ul> <li> prediction: in cases where X are readily available but the output Y cannot be easily obtained. <ul> <li><span class="math inline">\(\hat{Y}=\hat{f}(X)\)</span></li> <li> the accuracy of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{Y}\)</span> as a prediction of Y depends on two quantities: reducible error and irreducible error </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p> In general, <span class="math inline">\(\hat{f}\)</span> is not a perfect estimate for <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span>, and this inaccuracy will introduce some error. This error is reducible since we can potentially improve the accuracy of <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> by using the most appropriate technique. However, since Y is a function of <span class="math inline">\(\epsilon\)</span>, which by definition, cannot be predicted using X, and this is known as the irreducible error. </p> <p> Why is the irreducible error larger than zero? The quantity <span class="math inline">\(\epsilon\)</span> may contain unmeasured variables that are useful in predicting Y. The focus of this book is on techniques for estimating <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> with the aim of minimizing the reducible error. </p> <ul> <li> <p> inference: We now are interested in understanding the association between Y and <span class="math inline">\(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_p\)</span>. In this situation, we wish to estimate <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span>, but our goal is not to make predictions for Y. Therefore, <span class="math inline">\(\hat{f}\)</span> cannot be treated as a black box because we need to know its exact form. </p> <ul> <li>which predictors are associated with the response?</li> <li>what is the relationship between the response and each predictor?</li> <li> Can the relationship between Y and each predictor be adequately summarized using a linear equation, or is the relationship more complicated? </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="how-do-we-estimate-f" class="section level4"> <h4>How do we estimate f?</h4> <ul> <li> <p>parametric methods: involve a two-step model-based approach</p> <ul> <li> first, we make an assumption about the functional form, or shape of <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span>. for example, we assume <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> is linear: </li> </ul> <p><span class="math display">\[ f(X)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p \]</span></p> </li> </ul> <p> instead of estimating the black-box function <span class="math inline">\(f(X)\)</span>, we only need to estimate <span class="math inline">\(p+1\)</span> coefficients <span class="math inline">\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p\)</span>. * second, we need a procedure to train our model using training data, that is we want to find values of estimates of parameters such that </p> <p><span class="math display">\[ Y \approx \beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p \]</span></p> <p>the most common approach to fitting/training the <em>linear model</em> is referred to as <em>(ordinary) least squares</em>.</p> <p> The model-based approach is referred to as parametric: it reduces the problem of estimating f down to one of estimating a set of parameters. Assuming a parametric form for f simplifies the problem of estimating f because it is generally much easier to estimate a set of parameters than it is to fit an entirely arbitrary function f. The downside of parametric approach is that the model we choose will usually not match the true unknown form of f. If the choice of f is too off, then the estimate will be poor. To overcome this, we can choose flexible models that can fit many different possible functional forms for f. But in general, fitting a flexible model requires estimating a greater number of parameters, which can lead to a phenomenon known as <strong>overfitting</strong> the data, meaning they follow the error o noise too closely. </p> <ul> <li>non-parametric methods: no assumption about the functional form of f</li> </ul> <p> Instead, they seek an estimate of f that gets as close to the data points as possible. The advantage over parametric approach is by avoiding the assumption of a particular form for f, they have the potential to accurately fit a wider range of possible shapes for f. But non-parametric approaches do suffer from a major disadvantage: since they do not reduce the problem of estimating f to a small number of parameters,<em>a very large number of observations</em> is required in order to obtain an accurate estimate for f, such as <strong>splines</strong>. </p> </div> <div id="the-trade-off-between-prediction-accuracy-and-model-interpretability" class="section level4"> <h4>The trade-off between prediction accuracy and model interpretability</h4> <p> Why choosing inflexible method instead of a very flexible approach? * when inference is the goal, linear model may be a good choice since it is quite easy to understand the relationship between Y and X; in contrast, flexible approaches, such as splines and boosting methods can lead to such complicated estimates of f that it is difficult to understand how any individual predictors is associated with the response. </p> <div class="float"> <img src="%22flexibilit-interpretability.png%22" alt="trade-off."/> <div class="figcaption">trade-off.</div> </div> </div> <div id="supervised-vs.-unsupervised" class="section level4"> <h4>supervised vs. unsupervised</h4> <ul> <li> supervised <ul> <li>linear regression</li> <li>logisitic regression</li> <li>GAM</li> <li>boosting</li> <li>support vector machines</li> </ul> </li> <li> unsupervised <ul> <li>clustering</li> </ul> </li> <li> semi-supervised learning <ul> <li>for part of the observations, we don’t have response</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="regression-vs.-classification" class="section level4"> <h4>regression vs. classification</h4> <p>There is no clear-cut distinction:</p> <ul> <li>we tend to refer to problems with a quantitative response as regression problems</li> <li>those involving qualitative response as classification problems</li> </ul> <p> Least squares linear regression is used with a quantitative response, where as logistic regression is typically used with a qualitative response (binary). Thus, despite its name, logistic regression is a classification method. But since it estimates class probabilities, it can be thought of as a regression method as well. </p> <p> We tend to select statistical methods based on the fact that if the response is quantitative or qualitative. However, whether the predictors are qualitative or quantitative is generally considered less important, provided that ant qualitative predictors are properly coded before analysis is performed. </p> </div> </div> <div id="assessing-model-accuracy" class="section level3"> <h3>Assessing model accuracy</h3> <p> There is no free lunch in statistics: no one method dominates all others over all possible data sets. Hence, it is an important task to decide for any given set of data which method produces the best results. </p> <div id="measuring-the-quality-of-fit" class="section level4"> <h4>measuring the quality of fit</h4> <p> To measure the performance of a statistical learning method on a given data set, we need some ways to measure how well its predictions actually <em>match</em> the observed data. That is, we need to quantify the extent to which the predicted response value for a given observation is close to the true response value for that observation. </p> <p> in regression setting, the most commonly-used measure is the mean squared error (<strong>MSE</strong>): <span class="math display">\[ MSE=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{f}(x_1))^2 \]</span> * training MSE * test MSE: we care about this! </p> <p> When a given method yields a small training MSE but a large test MSE, we are said to be overfitting the data. That is, our statistical learning procedure is working too hard to find patterns in the training data and may be picking up some patterns that are just caused by random chance rather than by true properties of the unknown function of f. </p> </div> <div id="bias-variance-trade-off" class="section level4"> <h4>bias-variance trade-off</h4> <p> The expected test MSE, for a given value <span class="math inline">\(x_0\)</span>, can always be decomposed into the sum of three fundamental quantities:<br/> * the variance of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{f}(x_0)\)</span> * the squared bias of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{f}(x_0)\)</span> * the variance of the error </p> <p> A good statistical learning method would simultaneously achieve low variance and low bias. * variance: the amount by which <span class="math inline">\(\hat{f}\)</span> would change if we estimate it using a different training data set.
