Since the training data are used to fit the statistical learning method different <em>training</em> data sets will result in a different <span class="math inline">\(\hat{f}\)</span>. If a method has high variance then small changes in the training data can result in large changes in <span class="math inline">\(\hat{f}\)</span>. In general, more flexible statistical methods have higher variance. </p> <ul> <li> bias: the error introduced by approximating a real-life problem by a much simpler model. Generally, more flexible methods result in less bias. </li> </ul> <p> As a general rule, as we use more flexible methods, the variance will increase and the bias will decrease. The relative rate of change of these two quantities determines whether the test MSE increases or decreases. </p> <p> The relationship between bias, variance, and test MSE is referred to as the bias-variance trade-off. Good test set performance of a statistical leanring method required low variance as well as low squared biasa. The challenge lies in finding a method for which both the variance and the squared bias are low. in a real-life case in which <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> is unobserbed, it is generally not possible to explicitly compute the test MSE, bia, or variance for a statistical learning method. Nevertheless, we should alway keep in mind the bias-variacne trade-off. Cross-validation, which is a way to estimate the test MSE using the training data. Bias-variance trade-off transfer to the classification setting with only some modifications. </p> </div> <div id="classification-setting" class="section level4"> <h4>classification setting</h4> <ul> <li>training error rate</li> <li>test error rate</li> </ul> <p> Suppose that we seek to estimate f on the basis of training observations <span class="math inline">\({(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n,y_n)}\)</span>, where <span class="math inline">\(y_1, \dots, y_n\)</span> are qualitative. The most common approach for quantifying the accuracy of our estimate f is the <em>training error rate</em>, the proportion of mistakes that are made if we apply our estimate <span class="math inline">\(\hat{f}\)</span> to the training observations: </p> <p><span class="math display">\[ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(y_i\ne\hat{y_i}) \]</span></p> <p> I is an indicator variable that equals 1 if observed y does not euqal predicted y and 0 if it does. A good classifier is one for which the <em>test error rate</em> is smallest </p> <p><span class="math display">\[ Ave(I(y_0\ne\hat{y_0})) \]</span></p> <p> The Bayes classifier: we should simply assign a test observation with predictor vector <span class="math inline">\(x_0\)</span> to the class j for which <span class="math display">\[ Pr(Y=j|X=x_0) \]</span> is largest. This is a conditional probability and it is the probability that Y=j given the observed predictor vector <span class="math inline">\(x_0\)</span>. This very simple classifier is called <strong>Bayes classifier</strong>. in a two-class problem where there are only two possible response values, the Bayes classifier corresponds to predicting class one if <span class="math inline">\(Pr(Y=1|X=x_0)>0.5\)</span>, and class two otherwise. </p> <p> K-nearest Neighbors: * in theory, we would always like to predict qualitative responses using the Bayes classifier. But for real data, we do not know the conditional distribution of Y given X, and so computing the Bayes classifier is impossible. That means, the Bayes classifier serves as an unattainable gold standard against which to compare other methods. * K-nearest neighbors (KNN), like many other approaches, attempts to estiamte the conditional distribution of Y given X. Despite KNN is a very simple approach, it can often produce classifiers that are surprisingly close to the optimal Bayes classifier. </p> </div> </div> </div> <div id="chap-3.-linear-regression" class="section level2"> <h2>chap 3. Linear regression</h2> <div id="estimatig-the-coefficients" class="section level3"> <h3>estimatig the coefficients</h3> <p> Let <span class="math inline">\(\hat{y_i}=\hat{\beta_0}+\hat{\beta_1}x_i\)</span> be the prediction for Y based on the ith value of X. Then <span class="math inline">\(e_i=y_i-\hat{y_i}\)</span> represents the ith residual. We define the residual sum of squares (RSS) as: </p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ RSS=e^2_1+e^2_2+\dots+e^2_n \]</span> The least squares approach chooses <span class="math inline">\(\hat{beta_0}, \hat{beta_1}\)</span> to minimize the RSS. </p> </div> <div id="assess-the-accuracy-of-coefficient-estiamtes" class="section level3"> <h3>assess the accuracy of coefficient estiamtes</h3> <p> Notice that different data sets generated from the same true model result in slightly different least squares lines, but the unobserved population regression line does not change. How accurate is the sample mean <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}\)</span> as an estimate of <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span>? We have established that the average of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}\)</span>s over many data sets will be very close to <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span>, but that a single estimate <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}\)</span> may be a substantial underestimate or overestimate of <span class="math inline">\(\mu\)</span>. </p> <ul> <li>How far off will that single estimate of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}\)</span> be?</li> </ul> <p> In general, we answer this question by computing the standard error of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}\)</span>, written as SE(<span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mu}\)</span>). We have the well-known formula: </p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ Var(\hat{\mu})=SE(\hat{\mu})^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{n} \]</span> The estimate of <span class="math inline">\(sigma\)</span> is known as the residual standard error (RSE), and is given by: <span class="math display">\[ RSE=\sqrt{RSS/(n-2)}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y_i})^2} \]</span> </p> <ul> <li>Standard errors can be used to construct confidence intervals.</li> <li>Standard error can be used to perform hypothesis tests.</li> </ul> </div> <div id="assess-the-accuracy-of-the-model" class="section level3"> <h3>assess the accuracy of the model</h3> <p> The quality of a linear regression fit is typically assessed using two related quantities * residual standard error * <span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span> </p> <p> The RSE is considered an absolute measure of the lack of fit of the linear model to data. If the predictions obtained using the model are very close to the true outcome values, then the RSE will be small; otherwise, RSE will be large. </p> <p> <span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span> statistics provides an alternative measure of fit. It takes the form of a proportion-the proportion of variance explained-and so it always takes on a value between 0 and 1, and is independent of the scale of Y. </p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ R^2=\frac{TSS-RSS}{TSS}=1-\frac{RSS}{TSS} \]</span> The <span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span> has an interpretational advantage over the RSE, since it always takes value between 0 and 1; however, it can still be challenging to determine what is a good <span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span>. </p> </div> <div id="multiple-linear-regression" class="section level3"> <h3>multiple linear regression</h3> <p>linear regression model takes the form <span class="math display">\[ Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p+\epsilon \]</span></p> <p> We interpret <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j\)</span> as the average effect on Y of a one unit increase in <span class="math inline">\(X_j\)</span> , holding all other predictors fixed. </p> <div id="estimating-the-regression-coefficients" class="section level4"> <h4>estimating the regression coefficients</h4> <p> We choose <span class="math inline">\(\beta_0, \beta_1,\dots,\beta_p\)</span> to minimize the <strong>sum of squared residuals</strong>. </p> </div> <div id="some-important-questions" class="section level4"> <h4>some important questions</h4> <p>when performing multiple linear regression, we usually are interested in answering a few important questions:</p> <ul> <li> is at least one of the predictors useful in predicting the response? <ul> <li>F-test</li> </ul> </li> <li> do all the predictors help to explain Y, or is only a subset of the predictors useful? <ul> <li>forward selection</li> <li>backward selection</li> <li>mixed selection</li> </ul> </li> <li> how well does the model fit the data? <ul> <li>RSE</li> <li><span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span></li> </ul> </li> <li> given a set of predictor values, what response value should we predict, and how accurate is our prediction? <ul> <li>confidence intervals</li> <li>prediction intervals</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> </div> <div id="other-considerations-in-the-regression-model" class="section level3"> <h3>other considerations in the regression model</h3> <div id="qualitative-predictors" class="section level4"> <h4>qualitative predictors</h4> <p> So far, we have assumed that all variables in our linear regression model are quantitative. In practise, this is not necessarily the case. </p> <ul> <li>predictors with two levels: indicator or dummy variables using one-hot encoding</li> <li>qualitative predictors with more than two levels</li> </ul> </div> <div id="extensions-of-the-linear-model" class="section level4"> <h4>extensions of the linear model</h4> <ul> <li> additive: we assume the association between a predictor <span class="math inline">\(X_j\)</span> and the response Y does not depend on the values of the other predictors </li> <li> linear: the change in response associated with a one-unit change in <span class="math inline">\(X_j\)</span> is constant, regardless of the value of <span class="math inline">\(X_j\)</span>. </li> </ul> <p> interaction term. non-linear relationship: polynomial functional form. * collinearity: correlation matrix for pairs; better way using variance inflation factor(VIF) * outliers: unusual <span class="math inline">\(y_i\)</span> * high leverage: unusual <span class="math inline">\(x_i\)</span> </p> </div> </div> </div> <div id="chap-4.-classification" class="section level2"> <h2>chap 4. Classification</h2> <p> There are many classification techniques or classifier: <em>logistic regression, linear discriminant analysis, quadratic discriminant analysis, naive Bayes, and K-nearest neighbors</em>.<br/> * The discussion of logistic regression is used as a jumping-off point for a discussion of generalized linear models, and in particular, Poisson regression. * more computer-intensive classification methods: <em>generalized additive methods, tree, random forests</em>, and <em>boosting</em>; and <em>support vector machines</em> </p> <div id="why-not-linear-regression" class="section level3"> <h3>Why not linear regression?</h3> <p> Suppose we have a qualitative response with three levels: stroke, drug overdose, and epileptic seizure. We could consider encoding these values as a quantitative response variables as follows: </p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ Y= \begin{cases} {1}, & \text{if stroke;} \\ {2}, & \text{if drug overdose;} \\ {3}, & \text{if epileptic serzure.} \\ \end{cases} \]</span> </p> <p> Least squares could be used to fit a linear regression model to predict Y on the basis of a set of predictors. However, this enconding implies an ordering on the outcomes, rendering drug overdose in between stroke and epileptic seizure and insisting that the difference between stroke and drug overdose is the same as the difference between drug overdose and epileptic seizure. In practice, there is no particular reason that this needs to be the case. </p> <p> Even with only two classes, say a binary response with 0/1 coding where least squares is not completely unreasonable, a regression method has some problems: it can be shown that the <span class="math inline">\(X\hat{\beta}\)</span> obtained using linear regression is an estimate of the probability of Y given X in this case. However, if we use linear regression, some of our estimates might be outside the [0,1] interval, making them hard to interpret as probabilities. </p> <p> There are at least two reasons not to perform classification using a regression method:<br/> * a regression method cannot accommodate a qualitative response with more than two classes * a regression method will not provide meaningful estimate of Pr(Y|X), even with just two classes. </p> </div> <div id="logistic-regression" class="section level3"> <h3>logistic regression</h3> <p>logistic regression models the probability of Y given X, which can be written as</p> <p> <span class="math display">\[ p(X)=Pr(Y=1|X) \]</span> The values of p(X) will range between 0 and 1, then for any given value of X, a prediction can be made for Y. </p> <div id="the-logistic-model" class="section level4"> <h4>The logistic model</h4> <p> How should we model the relationship between <span class="math inline">\(p(X)=Pr(Y=1|X)\)</span> and X? we consider using a linear regression model to represent these probabilities: <span class="math display">\[ p(X)=\beta_0+\beta_1X \]</span> </p> <p> The problem with this approach is that with for X close to 0, we predict a negative probability of Y; if we were to predict for very large X, we would get values bigger than 1. These predictions are not sensible, since the true probabilities must fall between 0 and 1. </p> <p> To avoid this problem, we must model p(X) using a function that gives outputs between 0 and 1 for all values of X. There are many candidate functions that meet this criteria. In logistic regression, we use the <strong>logistic function</strong>: <span class="math display">\[ p(X)=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1X}}{1+e^{\beta_0+\beta_1X}} \]</span> To fit the model, we use a method called <em>maximum likelihood</em>. We rewrite the logistic function: <span class="math display">\[ \frac{p(X)}{1-p(X)}=e^{\beta_1+\beta_1X} \]</span> </p> <p> The quantity <span class="math inline">\(\frac{p(X)}{1-p(X)}\)</span> is called odds, taking the range from <span class="math inline">\([0, \infty]\)</span>. By taking the logarithm of both sides, we arrive at <span class="math display">\[ log(\frac{p(X)}{1-p(X)})=\beta_1+\beta_1X \]</span> The left-hand side is called the <strong>log odds</strong> or <strong>logit</strong>. We see that the logistic regression model has a logit that is linear in X. What we can observe from the relationship between p(X) and X are: </p> <ul> <li><p>the relationship is not linear</p></li> <li><p>the change in p(X) caused by one unit change in X depends on the actual value of X</p></li> <li> <p>p(X) and X is positively associated if <span class="math inline">\(\beta_1\)</span> is positive; and vice versa.</p> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="estimating-the-regression-coefficients-1" class="section level4"> <h4>estimating the regression coefficients</h4> <p> The coefficients are unknown and must be estimated based on available training data. non-linear least squares can be used to fit the model but maximum likelihood is preferred because of its better statistical properties. We seek estimates for <span class="math inline">\(\beta_0, \beta_1\)</span> such that the predicted probability <span class="math inline">\(\hat{p}(x_i)\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(x_i\)</span> for each individual corresponds as closely as to the individual’s observed X status. In other words, we try to find such estimates that plugging these estimates into the model for p(X) yields a number close to 1 for all individuals who are classified as group 1, and a number close to 0 for all individuals who are classified as group 0. Formulating it in mathematical equation in a <strong>likelihood function</strong>: <span class="math display">\[ \ell(\beta_0, \beta_1)=\prod_{i:y_i=1} p(x_i)\prod_{i':y_{i'}=1}(1-p(x_{i'})) \]</span> The estimates <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\beta}_0\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\beta_1}\)</span> are chosen to maximize this likelihood function. maximum likelihood is a very general approach that is used to fit many of the non-linear models. In the linear regression setting, the least squares approach is a special case of maximum likelihood. One can use qualitative predictors with the logistic regression model using the dummy variable approach. </p> </div> <div id="multiple-logistic-regression" class="section level4"> <h4>multiple logistic regression</h4> <p> The results obtained using one predictor may be different from those obtained using multiple predictors when there is correlation among the predictors. In general, the phenomenon is known as <strong>confounding</strong>. </p> </div> <div id="multinomial-logistic-regression" class="section level4"> <h4>multinomial logistic regression</h4> <p> when we have a response variable with more than two levels, we extend the two-level case to multinomial logistic regression. To do this, we first select a single level (the Kth level) to serve as the baseline, and then we rewrite the model : <span class="math display">\[ Pr(Y=k|X=x)=\frac{e^{\beta_{k0}+\beta_{k1}x_1+\dots+\beta_{kp}x_p}}{1+\sum_{l=1}^{K-1}e^{\beta_{l0}+\beta_{l1}x_1+\dots+\beta_{lp}x_p}} \]</span> for <span class="math inline">\(k=1,\dots,K-1\)</span>, and <span class="math display">\[ Pr(Y=K|X=x)=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{l=1}^{K-1}e^{\beta_{l0}+\beta_{l1}x_1+\dots+\beta_{lp}x_p}} \]</span> it can be shown that for <span class="math inline">\(k=1,\dots,K-1\)</span>: <span class="math display">\[ log\frac{Pr(Y=k|X=x)}{Pr(Y=K|X=x)}=\beta_{k0}+\beta_{k1}x_1+\dots+\beta_{kp}x_p \]</span> This equation again indicates that the log odds between any pair of classes is linear in the features/predictors. </p> </div> </div> <div id="generative-models-for-classification" class="section level3"> <h3>generative models for classification</h3> <p> In statistical jargon, we model the the conditional distribution of the response Y given the predictors. We now consider an alternative and less direct approach to estimating these probabilities. Now we model the distribution of the predictors X separately in each of the response classes, and then use Bayes’ theorem to flip these around into estimates for Pr(Y=k|X=x). </p> <p> why do we need another method when we already have logistic regression? * when there is substantial separation between the two classes, the parameters for the logistic regression model are surprisingly unstable. * if the distribution of the predictors X is approximately normal in each of the classes and the sample size is small, then the new approaches may be more accurate than logistic regression. * the new methods can be naturally extended to the case of more than two response levels. </p> <p> suppose we wish to classify an observation into one of K (<span class="math inline">\(\ge2\)</span>) classes, meaning the qualitative response Y can take on K possible distinct and un-ordered values. Let <span class="math inline">\(\pi_k\)</span> denote the prior probability that a randomly chosen observation comes from the kth class, and <span class="math inline">\(f_k(X)=Pr(X|Y=k)\)</span> denote the density function of X for an observation that comes from the kth class. According to Bayes’ theorem: <span class="math display">\[ Pr(Y=k|X=x)=\frac{\pi_kf_k(x)}{\sum_{l=1}^{K}\pi_lf_l(x)} \]</span> this is the posterior probability that an observation <span class="math inline">\(X=x\)</span> belongs to the kth class. That is, it is the probability that the observation belongs to the kth class, given the predictor value for that observation. The posterior probability equation suggests that instead of directly computing the posterior probability, we can simply plug in estimates of <span class="math inline">\(\pi_k\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(f_k(x)\)</span> into it. In general, estimating <span class="math inline">\(\pi_k\)</span> is easy if we have a random sample from the population: we simply compute the fraction of the training observations that belong to the kth class. However, estimating the density function <span class="math inline">\(f_k(x)\)</span> is much more challenging. </p> <div id="classifiers-with-different-estimates-of-the-density-function" class="section level4"> <h4>classifiers with different estimates of the density function</h4> <ul> <li> linear discriminant analysis for p=1 <ul> <li>assumption: <span class="math inline">\(f_k(x)\)</span> is normal or Gaussian</li> <li>estimates omitted</li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p> LDA classifier plugs in the estimates and assigns an observation <span class="math inline">\(X=x\)</span> to the class for which <span class="math display">\[ \hat{\delta}(x)=x\frac{\hat{\mu_k}}{\hat{\sigma^2}}-\frac{\hat{\mu^2_k}}{\hat{2\sigma^2}}+log(\hat{\pi}_k) \]</span> is largest. The word <em>linear</em> in the classifier’s name stems from the fact that the <strong>discriminant function</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\delta}(x)\)</span> are linear function of x as compared to a more complex form of x. </p> <ul> <li> linear discriminant analysis for p>1 <ul> <li> assumption: we assume that <span class="math inline">\(\vec{X}=(X_1, \dots, X_p)\)</span> is drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution, with a class-specific mean vector and a common covariance matrix. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p> The multivariate Gaussian distribution assumes that each individual predictor follows a one-dimensional normal distribution, with some correlation between each pair of predictors. Put it in mathematical term, we write <span class="math inline">\(X \sim N(\mu, \mathbb{\Sigma})\)</span>. here <span class="math inline">\(E(X)=\mu\)</span> is the mean of X (a vector of p components), and <span class="math inline">\(Cov(X)=\mathbb{\Sigma}\)</span> is the <span class="math inline">\(p \times p\)</span> covariance matrix of X. </p> <p> in practise, a binary classifier can make two types of errors: * incorrectly assign an individual who belongs to class 1 to class 2 * incorrectly assign an individual of class 2 to class 1 </p> <p>A <strong>confusion matrix</strong> is a convenient way to display this information.</p> <ul> <li>sensitivity: the percentage of true class Yes that are predicted</li> <li>specificity: the percentage of class No that are correctly identified</li> </ul> <p> The Bayes classifier works by assigning an observation to the class for which the posterior probability <span class="math inline">\(p_k(X)\)</span> is greatest. In the two-class case this amounts to assigning an observation to class 1 if the posterior probability of class 1 is greater than 0.5. However, if we are concerned about the incorrectly predicting the class 1 status for individuals who belong to class 1, then we can consider lowering the threshold. Choice on the best threshold must be based on domain knowledge, such as detailed information about the costs associated with class 1. </p> <p> <strong>ROC</strong> curve is a popular graphic for simultaneously displaying two types of errors for all possible thresholds. ROC is an acronym for receiver operating characteristics.The overall performance of a classifier, summarized over all possible thresholds, is given by the area under the ROC curve (AUC). An ideal ROC curve will hug the top left corner, so the larger the AUC the better the classifier. We expect a classifier that performs no better than chance to have an AUC of 0.5 on test sets. ROC curves are useful for comparing different classifiers since they take into account all possible thresholds. </p> <p> When we apply a classifier, possible results are:<br/> * true positive (TP) and true negative (TN) * false positive (FP) and false negative (FN) </p> <ul> <li>false positive rate = FP/N, type I error, 1-specificity</li> <li>true positive rate = TP/P, 1-type II error, power, sensitivity</li> <li>positive predicted value: TP/P*, precision, 1-false discovery proportion</li> <li>negative predicted value: TN/N*</li> </ul> </div> <div id="quadratic-discriminant-analysis" class="section level4"> <h4>quadratic discriminant analysis</h4> <p> LDA assumes that the observations within each class are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution withi a class specific mean vector and a covariance matrix that is common to all K classes. Quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA) provides an alternative approach. </p> <ul> <li>assumption: observations are drawn from a Gaussian distribution</li> <li>unlike LDA, QDA assumes that each class has its own covariance matrix.</li> </ul> <p> that is, QDA assumes that an observation from the kth class is of the form <span class="math inline">\(X \sim N(\mu_k, \Sigma_k)\)</span>, where <span class="math inline">\(\Sigma_k\)</span> is a covariance matrix for the kth class. For QDA, the quantity x appears as a quadratic function in the <strong>discriminant function</strong>. this is where QDA gets its name. </p> <p> Why assuming different covariance matrices for different classes of Y? or why prefer LDA over QDA? The answer lies in the bias-variance trade-off. </p> <ul> <li> when there are <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> predictors, then estimating a covariance matrix requires estimating <span class="math inline">\(p(p+1)/2\)</span> parameters. </li> <li> QDA estimates a separate covariance matrix for each class, for a total of <span class="math inline">\(Kp(p+1)/2\)</span> parameters. </li> <li>LDA estimates <span class="math inline">\(Kp\)</span> linear coefficients</li> </ul> <p> Consequently, LDA is a much less flexible classifier than QDA, and has substantially lower <strong>variance</strong>, which could potentially lead to improved prediction performance. However, if the K classes share a common covariance matrix is badly off, then LDA can suffer from high bias. </p> <p> In general, LDA tends to be a better bet than QDA if there are relatively few training observations and so reducing variance is crucial. QDA is recommended if the training data set is very large where the variance of the classifier is not a major concern, or the assumption of a common covariance matrix for all K classes is clearly untenable. </p> </div> <div id="naive-bayes" class="section level4"> <h4>naive Bayes</h4> <p> naive Bayes classifier takes a different tract for estimating <span class="math inline">\(f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_K(x)\)</span>. Instead of assuming that these functions belong to a particular family of distributions, e.g., multivariate normal distribution, it makes a single assumption: within the kth class, the p predictors are independent. </p> <p> Stated mathematically, this assumption means that for <span class="math inline">\(k=1,\dots, K\)</span>, <span class="math display">\[ f_k(x)=f_{k1}(x_1) \times f_{k2}(x_2) \times \dots \times f_{kp}(x_p) \]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(f_{kj}\)</span> is the density function of the jth predictor among observations in the kth class. This is a powerful assumption. Essentially, estimating a p-dimensional density function is challenging because we must consider not only the marginal distribution of each predictor-that is the distribution of each predictor on its own-but also the joint distribution of the predictors-that is, the association among different predictors. in the case of multivariate normal distribution, the association among predictors is summarized by the off-diagonal elements of the covariance matrix. However, in general, this association can be hard to characterize, and exceedingly challenging to estimate. by assuming independence of predictors, we completely eliminate the worry about the association. </p> <p> In most settings, we do not believe the naive Bayes assumption that all predictors are independent. Essentially, the naive Bayes assumption introduces some bias, but reduces variance, leading to a classifier that works quite well in practise as a result of <strong>bias-variance trade-off</strong>. When p is large or n is small, naive Bayes relative to LDA or QDA presents a greater pay-off in where reducing variance is very important. </p> </div> </div> <div id="comparison-of-classification-methods" class="section level3"> <h3>comparison of classification methods</h3> <p> To compare performance of LDA, QDA, naive Bayes, and logistic regression, we consider these approaches in a setting with K classes, so that we assign an observation to the class that maximizes Pr(Y=k|X=x). Equivalently, we can set K as the baseline class and assign an observation to the class that maximizes <span class="math display">\[ log\frac{Pr(Y=k|X=x)}{Pr(Y=K|X=x)} \]</span> for <span class="math inline">\(k=1,\dots,K\)</span>. </p> <p>comparison</p> <ul> <li> LDA is a special case of QDA with <span class="math inline">\(c_{kjl}=0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(j, l=1, \dots, p, k=1,\dots,K\)</span>, which is not surprising since LDA is simply a restricted version of QDA with <span class="math inline">\(\Sigma_1=\Sigma_2=\dots=\Sigma_K=\Sigma\)</span>. </li> <li> Any classifier with a linear decision boundary is a special case of naive Bayes with <span class="math inline">\(g_{kj}(x_j)=b_{kj}(x_j)\)</span>. This means LDA is a special case of naive Bayes. </li> <li>naive Bayes is a special case of LDA with p=1.</li> <li> neither QDA nor naive Bayes is a special case of the other. QDA has the potential to be more accurate in settings where interactions among predictors are important in discriminating classes. </li> </ul> <p> None of these methods dominates the others: in any setting, the choice of method will depend on the true distribution of the predictors in each of the K classes, as well as other considerations, such as the values of n and p. </p> <ul> <li> logistic regression: the posterior probability function is identical to that of LDA. We expect LDA to outperform logistic regression when the normality assumption (approximately) holds, and we expect logistic regression to perform better when it does not. </li> </ul> <div id="k-nearest-neighbors-knn" class="section level4"> <h4>K-nearest neighbors (KNN)</h4> <p> No assumptions are made in KNN so it’s a non-parametric approach: no assumptions are made about the shape of the decision boundary. </p> <ul> <li> because KNN is completely non-parametric, we can expect this approach to dominate LDA and logistic regression when the decision boundary is highly non-linear, provided that n is very large and p is small </li> <li>in order to provide accurate classification, KNN required a lot of observations relative to the number of predictors.</li> <li> in settings where the decision boundary is non-linear but n is only modest ,or p is not very small, QDA may be preferred to KNN because QDA can provide non-linear boundary while taking parametric forms, meaning it required a smaller sample size for accurate classification, relative to KNN. </li> <li> unlike logistic regression, KNN does not tell us which predictors are important: we don;t get a table of coefficients as from model summary of a logistic regression model. </li> </ul> </div> </div> <div id="generalized-linear-models" class="section level3"> <h3>generalized linear models</h3> <p> Sometimes we have response variable that are neither qualitative nor quantitative, rendering linear regression and classification untenable. Suppose we have counts of bikers as Y, problems fitting a linear regression model are: </p> <ul> <li>negative predictions</li> <li>violation of constant variance assumption</li> <li>continuous predictions instead of integers</li> </ul> <div id="poisson-regression" class="section level4"> <h4>Poisson regression</h4> <p> Suppose a random variable Y takes on non-negative integer values, and it follows the Poisson distribution, then <span class="math display">\[ Pr(Y=k)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}, k=0,1,2\dots \]</span> important properties of Poisson distribution are: <span class="math inline">\(E(Y)=Var(Y)=\lambda\)</span>. IN stead of modeling the count directly, we model the mean to vary as a function of the covariates. IN particular, we consider the following model for the mean <span class="math inline">\(\lambda=E(Y)\)</span>, which we write as <span class="math inline">\(\lambda(X_1,\dots,X_p)\)</span> to emphasize that it is a function of the covariates <span class="math inline">\(X_1,\dots,X_p\)</span>: <span class="math display">\[ log\lambda(X_1,\dots,X_p)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p \]</span> we take a log of <span class="math inline">\(\lambda(X_1,\dots,X_p)\)</span> to be linear in predictors in order to ensure that <span class="math inline">\(\lambda(X_1,\dots,X_p)\)</span> takes on non-negative values for all values of the covariates. To estimate the coefficients <span class="math inline">\(\beta_0,\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p\)</span>, we use the same maximum likelihood approach that we adopt for logistic regression. Specifically, given n observations from the Poisson regression model, the likelihood takes the form <span class="math display">\[ \ell(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots,\beta_p)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{e^{-\lambda(x_i)}\lambda(X_i)^{y_i}}{y_i!} \]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(\lambda(x_i)=e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\dots+\beta_px_{ip}}\)</span>. we estimate the coefficients that maximize the likelihood <span class="math inline">\(\ell(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots,\beta_p)\)</span>. </p> <ul> <li> interpretation: an increase in <span class="math inline">\(X_j\)</span> by one unit is associated with a change in <span class="math inline">\(E(Y)=\lambda\)</span> by a factor of <span class="math inline">\(exp(\beta_j)\)</span>.<br/> </li> <li> mean-variance relationship: by modeling with Poisson regression, we explicitly assume that, in Bike example, mean bike usage in a given hour equals the variance of bike usage during that hour. By contrast, under a linear regression model, the variance of bike usage always takes on constant value. IN general, Poisson regression model is able to handle the mean-variance relationship in a way that the linear regression model is not.<br/> </li> <li> non-negative fitted values: there are no negative predictions using the Poisson regression model. By contrast, when we fit a linear regression model to the Bike data set, almost 10% of the prediction are negative.<br/> </li> <li> over-dispersion: in the Bike example, the variance appears to be much higher than the mean, a situation referred to as over-dispersion. this cause the Z-values to be inflated. </li> </ul> </div> <div id="generalized-linear-models-in-greater-generality" class="section level4"> <h4>generalized linear models in greater generality</h4> <p>we have covered three types of regression models: linear, logistic, and Poisson. they share some characteristics:</p> <ul> <li> each approach uses predictors <span class="math inline">\(X_1, \dots, X_p\)</span> to predict a response Y. we assume that conditional on <span class="math inline">\(X_1, \dots, X_p\)</span>, Y belongs to a certain family of distributions. for linear regression, we typically assume that Y follows a Gaussian or normal distribution; for logistic regression, we assume that Y follows a Bernoulli distribution; for Poisson regression, we assume that Y follows a Poisson distribution.<br/> </li> <li> each approach models the mean of Y as a function of the predictors. in linear regression, the mean of Y takes the form <span class="math display">\[ E(Y|X_1, \dots, X_p)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p \]</span> i.e., it is a linear function of the predictors. For logistic regression, the mean takes the form <span class="math display">\[ E(Y|X_1, \dots, X_p)=Pr(Y=1|X_1, \dots, X_p)=\frac{e^{\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x_1+\dots+\beta_{p}x_p}}{1+e^{\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x_1+\dots+\beta_{p}x_p}} \]</span> </li> </ul> <p> while for Poisson regression it take the form <span class="math display">\[ E(Y|X_1, \dots, X_p)=\lambda(X_1, \dots, X_p)=e^{\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x_1+\dots+\beta_{p}x_p} \]</span> Equations above can be expressed using a <strong>link function</strong>, <span class="math inline">\(\eta\)</span>, which applies a transformation to <span class="math inline">\(E(Y|X_1, \dots, X_p)\)</span> so that the transformed mean is a linear function of the predictors. that is <span class="math display">\[ \eta(E(Y|X_1, \dots, X_p))=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x_1+\dots+\beta_{p}x_p \]</span> </p> <p>The link function for linear, logistic, and Poisson regression are</p> <ul> <li><span class="math inline">\(\eta(\mu)=\mu\)</span></li> <li><span class="math inline">\(\eta(\mu)=log(\frac{\mu}{1-\mu})\)</span></li> <li><span class="math inline">\(\eta(\mu)=log(\mu)\)</span></li> </ul> <p> The Gaussian, Bernoulli, and Poisson distributions are all members of a wider class of distributions, known as the <strong>exponential family</strong>. Other well-known members of this family include <strong>exponential distribution</strong>, the <strong>Gamma distribution</strong>, and the <strong>negative binomial distribution</strong>. In general, we can perform a regression by modeling the response Y as coming from a particular member of the exponential family, and then transforming the mean of the response so that the transformed mean is a linear function of the predictors via the link function. Any regression approach that allows this very general recipe is known as a generalized linear model (<strong>GLM</strong>). </p> </div> </div> </div> <div id="chap-5.-resampling" class="section level2"> <h2>chap 5. Resampling</h2> <p> Re-sampling methods are an indispensable tool in modern statistics. They involve repeatedly drawing samples from a training set and refitting a model on each sample to obtain additional information about the fitted model. </p> <p> For example, - to estimate the variability of a linear regression fit, we repeatedly draw different samples from the training data set, fit a linear regression to each new sample, and then examine the extend to which the resulting fits differ. - such information would not be available from fitting the model only once using the original training sample </p> <p>Two of most used re-sampling methods are</p> <ul> <li> cross-validation: used to estimate the test error associated with a given statistical learning method in order to evaluate its performance, or to select the appropriate level of flexibility. </li> <li>bootstrap: used to measure accuracy of a parameter estimate or a given statistical learning method.</li> </ul> <p> The process of evaluating a model’s performance is known as <strong>model assessment</strong>, whereas the process of choosing the proper level of flexibility for a model is known as <strong>model selection</strong>. </p> <div id="cross-validation" class="section level3"> <h3>cross-validation</h3> <ul> <li> test error rate: the average error that results from using a statistical learning method to predict the response on a new observation. </li> </ul> <p> The test error rate can be easily calculated if a designated test set is available. However, this is not usually the case. In contrast the training error rate can be obtained by applying the statistical learning method to the observations used in its training. </p> <ul> <li>training error rate: quite different from the test error rate, and can dramatically underestimate the test error rate.</li> </ul> <p> In the absence of ver large test set, a number of techniques can be used to estimate this quantity using available training data. <strong>Some</strong> make adjustments to the training error rate to estimate the test error rate; <strong>others</strong> achieve so by holding out a subset of the training observations from the fitting process, and then applying the statistical learning method to those held out observations. </p> <div id="validation-set-approach" class="section level4"> <h4>validation set approach</h4> <p> The validation set approach randomly divides the available set into two parts, a training set and a validation set or hold-out set. The statistical model is fit on the training set, and the fitted model is used to predict the responses for the observations in the validation set. The resulting validation set error rate-mean squared error in the case of quantitative response-provides an estimate of the test error rate. </p> <ul> <li> the validation estimate of the test error rate can be highly variable, depending on precisely which observations are included in the training set and which observations are included in the validation set.<br/> </li> <li> only observations included in the training set are used to fit the model. That is, only part of the original traning observations are used to fit the model. Statistical learning methods tend to perform worse when trained on fewer observations, which suggests that the validation set error rate may <strong>overestimate</strong> the test error rate for the model fit on the entire data set. </li> </ul> </div> <div id="cross-validation-1" class="section level4"> <h4>cross-validation</h4> <p>Cross-validation is a refinement of the validation set approach that addresses these two issues.</p> <div id="leave-one-out-cross-validation" class="section level5"> <h5>leave-one-out cross-validation</h5> <p> leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) is closely related to the validation set approach, but it attempts to address that method’s drawbacks. Like validation set approach, LOOCV involves splitting the set of observations into two parts. Instead of splitting the data set into two comparable subsets, LOOCV uses a single observation for validation, and the rest observations for training. That is, the statistical learning method is fit on the <span class="math inline">\(n-1\)</span> training observations, and a prediction <span class="math inline">\(\hat{y_i}\)</span> is made for the one held-out observation using its value <span class="math inline">\(x_i\)</span>. </p> <p> However, validation on a single observation is highly variable, so we repeat the procedure by <span class="math inline">\(n\)</span> times, and calculating <span class="math inline">\(n\)</span> MSE. The LOOCV estimate for the test MSE is the average of these <span class="math inline">\(n\)</span> test error estimates: <span class="math display">\[ \hat{MSE}=CV_{(n)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}MSE_i \]</span> LOOCV has major advantages over the validation set approach<br/> * far less bias: using as many as <span class="math inline">\(n-1\)</span> observations, LOOCV has variability as compared to fitting on almost half of the observations * validation set approach yields different results due to randomness in the training/validation set split, while performing LOOCV multiple will always yield the same result since there is no randomness in the training/validation set splits. </p> </div> <div id="k-fold-cross-validation" class="section level5"> <h5>k-fold cross-validation</h5> <p> K-fold cross-validation involves randomly dividing all observations into k groups, of approximately equal size. The first group/fold is used as the validation set, and the rest <span class="math inline">\(k-1\)</span> groups are used to train the statistical learning model. Then MSE is calculated for the held-out first set. Repeating this procedure <span class="math inline">\(k\)</span> times until all groups are used as validation set for once. This process produces <span class="math inline">\(k\)</span> estimates of test error, <span class="math inline">\(MSE_1, MSE_2,\dots, MSE_k\)</span>. we have <span class="math display">\[ CV_{(k)}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}MES_i \]</span> </p> <p> It is not hard to see LOOCV is a special case of k-fold cross-validation (CV) in which <span class="math inline">\(k\)</span> is set to equal <span class="math inline">\(n\)</span>. typically, we perform <span class="math inline">\(k=5\)</span> or <span class="math inline">\(k=10\)</span> CV. the advantage of doing this rather than <span class="math inline">\(k=n\)</span> is computational ease. LOOCV required fitting the statistical learning method n times, which could be computational expensive especially for algorithms with computational intensive procedures, and with extremely large number of observations. IN contrast, performing 10-fold CV requires fitting the learning procedure only ten times, which may be much more feasible.<br/> * moreover, although there is some variability in the CV estimates due to how observations are divided into ten folds, this variability is typically much lower than the variability in the test error estimates from the validation set approach. </p> <p> There are two scenarios in statistical learning process:<br/> * to determine how well a given statistical learning procedure can be expected on independent data * here, the actual estimate of the test MSE is of interest * where the minimum point of the estimated test MSE occurs? * here, the location of the minimum point in the estimated test MSE curve is important, but the actual value of the estimated test MSE is not. </p> </div> <div id="bias-variance-trade-off-for-k-fold-cross-validation" class="section level5"> <h5>bias-variance trade-off for k-fold cross-validation</h5> <p> In addition to advantage on computation, k-fold CV has another less obvious but potentially more important advantage over LOOCV. That is, k-fold CV often gives more accurate estimates of the test error rate than does LOOCV. This has to do with a <strong>bias-variance trade-off</strong>. </p> <p> Bias:<br/> * the validation set approach tends to <strong>overestimate</strong> the test error rate since the training set used to fit the statistical learning model contains only <strong>half</strong> of the observations. * LOOCV, in contrast, will give approximately unbiased estimates of test error, since each training set contains <span class="math inline">\(n-1\)</span> observations, which is almost as many as the number of the entire data set; * Performing k-fold CV (k<n) will lead to intermediate bias since each training set contains approximately <span class="math inline">\((k-1)k/n\)</span> observations-fewer than in the LOOCV approach. </p> <p> Therefore, from the perspective of <strong>bias</strong> reduction, LOOCV is to be preferred to k-fold CV. However, bias is not the only source of concern in an estimating procedure; we must consider the procedure’s variance. From variance perspective, LOOCV has higher variance than k-fold CV (k<n). Why? </p> <p> Variance:<br/> * the training sets in a LOOCV procedure are almost identical to each other and thus are correlated.<br/> * In contrast, k-fold CV has less similar training sets and smaller overlap between training sets.<br/> * In statistics, the mean of highly correlated quantities has higher variance than does the mean of quantities that are not highly correlated. This can be explained by the fact that when variables are highly correlated, they tend to move together in a similar direction. the individual deviations from the mean tend to align and reinforce each other. This results in a larger overall spread of the values around the mean, and therefore a higher variance. On the other hand, if the quantities are not highly correlated, their movements are more independent of each other. The deviations from their means are likely to cancel each other out to some extent when you take the mean of the quantities. </p> <p> To summarize, there is a bias-variance trade-off associated with the choice of k in the k-fold cross-validation. k=5 or k=10 has shown empirically to suffer neither from excessively high bias nor from very high variance. </p> </div> <div id="cross-validation-on-classification-problems" class="section level5"> <h5>cross-validation on classification problems</h5> <p> cross-validation is a very general technique that can be applied to not only regression problems, but also classification problems. In classification settings, instead of using MSE, we use the number of mis-classified observations. LOOCV error rate for example takes the form: <span class="math display">\[ CV_{(n)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Err_i \]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(Err_i=I(y_i \ne \hat{y}_i)\)</span>. K-fold CV error rate and validation error rate are defined analogously. </p> </div> </div> </div> <div id="bootstrap" class="section level3"> <h3>bootstrap</h3> <p> bootstrap is extremely powerful statistical tool that can be used to quantify the <strong>uncertainty</strong> associated with a given <strong>estimator</strong> or statistical learning method.<br/> * bootstrap can be used to estimate the <strong>standard errors</strong> of the <strong>coefficients</strong> from a linear regression fit. * bootstrap is powerful as it applied to a wide range of statistical learning methods for which a measure of variability is otherwise difficult to obtain and is not automatically output by statistical software. </p> <p> [<a href="example:\" class="uri">example:\\</a>](<a href="example:)%7B.uri%7D" class="uri">example:\</a> suppose we wish to invest into two financial assets that yield returns of X and Y, respectively, where X and Y are random quantities. We will invest a fraction <span class="math inline">\(\alpha\)</span> of our money in X, and will invest the remaining <span class="math inline">\(1-\alpha\)</span> in Y. Since there is variability associated with the returns on these two assets, we wish to choose <span class="math inline">\(\alpha\)</span> to minimize the total risk, or variance, of our investment. That is, we want to minimize <span class="math inline">\(Var(\alpha X+(1-\alpha)Y)\)</span> .It can be shown that the value that minimize the risk is given by <span class="math display">\[ \alpha=\frac{\alpha^2_Y-\alpha_{XY}}{\alpha^2_X+\alpha^2_Y-2\alpha_{XY}} \]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^2_X=Var(X), \alpha^2_Y=Var(Y), \alpha_{XY}=Cov(X,Y)\)</span>. </p> <p> in reality, the quantities <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^2_X, \alpha^2_Y, \alpha_{XY}\)</span> are unknown. We can compute estimates for these quantities, <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\alpha^2}_X,\hat{\alpha^2}_Y, \hat{\alpha}_{XY}\)</span>, using a data set that contains measurements for X and Y. we can then estimate the value <span class="math inline">\(\alpha\)</span> using <span class="math display">\[ \hat{\alpha}=\frac{\hat{\alpha^2}_Y-\hat{\alpha}_{XY}}{\hat{\alpha^2}_X+\hat{\alpha^2}_Y-2\hat{\alpha}_{XY}} \]</span> </p> <p> we simulate 100 pairs of returns for the investments X and Y, and then use these returns to estimate <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^2_X, \alpha^2_Y, \alpha_{XY}\)</span>., which we then substitute into the estimator equation to obtain estimates for <span class="math inline">\(\alpha\)</span>. </p> <p> It’s natural to wish to quantify the accuracy of our estimate of <span class="math inline">\(\alpha\)</span>. To estimate the standard deviation of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\alpha}\)</span>, we repeat the process of simulation 100 paired observations of X and Y, and estimating <span class="math inline">\(\alpha\)</span>, 1000 times. we then obtain 1000 estimates for <span class="math inline">\(\alpha\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\alpha_1}, \hat{\alpha_2}, \dots, \hat{\alpha_{1000}}\)</span>: we then calculate the mean and standard deviation of the estimates <span class="math display">\[ \begin{aligned} \bar{\alpha}=\frac{1}{1000}\sum_{i=1}^{1000}\hat{\alpha_i} \\ \rm SE_{\hat{\alpha}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{1000-1}\sum_{i=1}^{1000}(\hat{\alpha}_i-\bar{\alpha})^2} \end{aligned} \]</span> </p> <p> this gives us a very good idea of the accuracy of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\alpha}\)</span> by SE. we would expect <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\alpha}\)</span> to differ from <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\alpha}\)</span> by approximately SE, on average. </p> <p> In practice, however, the procedure estimating <span class="math inline">\(\rm SE(\hat{\alpha})\)</span> above cannot be applied, because we cannot generate new samples from the original population. this is where bootstrap comes into play. bootstrap allows us to use a computer to emulate the process of obtaining new sample sets, so that we can estimate the variability of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\alpha}\)</span> without generating additional samples. Here, instead of drawing independent samples/data sets repeatedly from the population, we obtain distinct data sets repeatedly sampling observations from the original data set. </p> <p> bootstrap can be used to estimated <span class="math inline">\(\rm SE\)</span>s of the regression coefficients, so how does it compare to the estimates obtained using <code>summary()</code> function or the standard formula (RSS)? In fact, bootstrap provides a more accurate estimate of the standard errors of the regression coefficients since it does not rely on assumptions of correct model specification or independence of observations. </p> </div> </div> <div id="chap-6.-linear-model-selection-and-regularization" class="section level2"> <h2>chap 6. linear model selection and regularization</h2> <p> linear model has distinct advantages in terms of inference, and on real-world problems, is often surprisingly competitive as compared to non-linear methods. </p> <p> In practice, assumptions for linear model are often violated. here we learn ways in which the simple linear model can be improved, by replacing least squared fitting with alternative fitting procedures. </p> <p> Why do we want to use another fitting procedure instead of least squares?<br/> alternative fitting procedures can yield better:<br/> * prediction accuracy * model interpretability </p> <ul> <li> <p> prediction accuracy: given that the true relationship is approximately linear, the least squares estimate will have low bias. When <span class="math inline">\(n \gg p\)</span>, then least squares estimates also have low variance. However, if the number of observations is not far more bigger than the number of predictors, then the least squares estimates can have a lot of variability. When <span class="math inline">\(n \le p\)</span>, then there is no longer a unique least squares estimate, and the method cannot be used at all. </p> </li> <li> <p> model interpretability: irrelevant variables lead to unnecessary complexity in resulting model, removing these variables-by setting the corresponding coefficient estimates to 0-we obtain a model that is more easily interpretable. </p> </li> </ul> <p> there are many alternatives to using least squares to fit <span class="math display">\[ Y = \beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p+\epsilon \]</span> </p> <ul> <li> <p> <code>subset selection</code>: this approach involves identifying a subset of predictors that are believed to be related to the response. we then fit the model using least squares on the reduced set of predictors </p> </li> <li> <p> <code>shrinkage</code>: this approach involves fitting a model using all predictors. However, the estimated coefficients are shrunken towards 0 relative to the least squares estimates. this shrinkage (aka <code>regularization</code>) has the effect of reducing variance. depending on what type of shrinkage is performed, some of the coefficients may be estimated to be exactly 0. therefore, shrinkage methods can also perform <code>variable selection</code>. </p> </li> <li> <p> dimension reduction: this approach involves projecting p predictors into an M-dimension subspace, where <span class="math inline">\(M \le p\)</span>. this can be achieved by computing M different linear combinations, or projections, of the p variables. then these M projections are used as predictors to fit the linear regression model by least squares. </p> </li> </ul> <div id="subset-selection" class="section level3"> <h3>subset selection</h3> <p>best subset + stepwise model selection procedures</p> <div id="best-subset-selection" class="section level4"> <h4>best subset selection</h4> <p> to perform best subset selection, we fit a separate least squares regression for each possible combination of the predictors. that is, we fit p models that contain one predictor, <span class="math inline">\(\binom{n}{k}=p(p-1)/2\)</span> models that contain exactly 2 predictors, and so forth. we then look at all of the resulting models to identify the best predictors. </p> <p>algorithms is described below:</p> <ul> <li> let <span class="math inline">\(M_o\)</span> denote the null model, with no predictors. this model simply predicts the sample mean for each observation. </li> <li> for <span class="math inline">\(k \in 1,2,\dots,p\)</span>: <ul> <li>fit all <span class="math inline">\(\binom{p}{k}\)</span> models that contain exactly k predictors</li> <li> pick the best among the <span class="math inline">\(\binom{p}{k}\)</span> models,a nd call it <span class="math inline">\(M_k\)</span>. best is defined as having the smallest residual sum of squares (RSS), or equivalently largest <span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span>-<strong>training error</strong>. </li> </ul> </li> <li> select a single best model from among <span class="math inline">\(M_0, \dots, M_p\)</span> using <code>cross-validated</code> <strong>test error</strong>, <span class="math inline">\(C_p(AIC), BIC,\)</span> or adjusted <span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span>. </li> </ul> <p> in the case of logistic regression, instead of ordering models by RSS in step 2, we use <strong>deviance</strong>, a measure that plays the role of RSS for a broader class of models. The deviance is negative 2 times the maximized log-likelihood; the smaller the deviance, the better the fit. </p> <p> disadvantage of best subset selection:<br/> * computational limitation: number of possible models (<span class="math inline">\(2^p\)</span>) grows rapidly as p increase. if <span class="math inline">\(p=10\)</span>, there are approximately 1000 possible models to be considered; if <span class="math inline">\(p=20\)</span>, then there are over one million possibilities. </p> <p> solution to computational challenge: step-wise selection. for computational reasons, best subset selection cannot be applied with very large p. </p> <div id="forward-stepwise-selection" class="section level5"> <h5>forward stepwise selection</h5> <p> forward stepwise selection is an alternative to best subset selection as it considers a much smaller set of models. forward stepwise selection starts with no predictors, and then adds predictors to the model, one at a time, until all of the predictors are in the model. In particular, at each step the variable that gives the greatest additional improvement to the fit is added to the model. </p> <p> best subset selection fits <span class="math inline">\(2^p\)</span> models, while forward stepwise selection fits only <span class="math inline">\(1+p(1+p)/2\)</span> models. when <span class="math inline">\(p=20\)</span>, best subset selection requires fitting 1,048,576 models, whereas forward stepwise selection requires fitting only 211 models, which is a substantial difference! </p> <ul> <li>disadvantage of forward stepwise selection: it is not guaranteed to find the best set of predictors</li> </ul> </div> <div id="backward-stepwise-selection" class="section level5"> <h5>backward stepwise selection</h5> <p> backward stepwise selection begins with the full least squares model containing all predictors, and then iteratively removes the lest useful predictor, one at a time. </p> </div> <div id="hybrid-approaches" class="section level5"> <h5>hybrid approaches</h5> <p> forward + backward stepwise selection: after adding each new variable, the method may also remove any variables that no longer provide an improvement to the model fit. such approach attempts to closely mimic best subset selection while maintaining the computational advantages of forward and backward stepwise selection. </p> </div> </div> <div id="choosing-the-optimal-model" class="section level4"> <h4>choosing the optimal model</h4> <p>to use above methods to select the best model, we need a way to determine which of these models is best.</p> <p> note from chapter 2, training error is a poor estimate of test error. therefore training RSS and <span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span> are not suitable for selecting the best model among a collection of models with different numbers of predictors since they are related to training error. </p> <p>to select the best model with respect to test error, we need to estimate test error. there are two common approaches:</p> <ul> <li> indirectly estimate test error by adjusting to the training error to account for the bias due to over-fitting. <ul> <li><span class="math inline">\(C_p\)</span></li> <li>AIC</li> <li>BIC</li> <li>adjusted <span class="math inline">\(R^2\)</span></li> </ul> </li> <li> directly estimate the test error, using either a validation set approach or a cross-validation approach. <ul> <li> problem with using validation set approach and cross-validation approach is that by changing the validation set or using another k-fold split, the precise best model will change. </li> <li> solution: select the model using the <code>one-standard-error</code> rule. we first calculate the standard error of the estimated test MSE (RSS/n) for each model size, and then select the smallest model for which the estimated test error is within one standard error of the lowest point on the curve. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> </div> <div id="shrinkage-methods" class="section level3"> <h3>shrinkage methods</h3> <p> subset selection methods involve selecting a subset of predictors and then using least squares to fit a linear model that contains a subset of predictors. An alternative to it is fitting a model <code>containing</code> all p predictors using a technique that constrain or <code>regularizes</code> the coefficient estimates, or equivalently, that <code>shrinks</code> the coefficient estimates towards 0. </p> <p> The two best-known techniques for shrinking the regression coefficients towards 0 are <strong>ridge regression</strong> and <strong>lasso</strong>. </p> <div id="ridge-regression" class="section level4"> <h4>ridge regression</h4> <p> recall that the least squares fitting procedure estimates <span class="math inline">\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p\)</span> to minimize <span class="math display">\[ \rm RSS= \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\beta_0-\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij})^2 \]</span> </p> <p> ridge regression is similar to least squares, except that the coefficients are estimated to minimize a slightly different quantity <span class="math display">\[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\beta_0-\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij})^2+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta^2_j=\rm RSS + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta^2_j \]</span> where <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \ge 0\)</span> is a tuning parameter, to be determined separately. this equation trades off two different criteria:<br/> - as with least squares, ridge regression seeks to minimize RSS - the second term, called <strong>shrinkage penalty</strong>, is small when <span class="math inline">\(\beta_1, \dots, \beta_p\)</span> are close to 0. the tuning parameter <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> serves to control the relative impact of these two terms on the regression coefficient estimates. </p> <p> as <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \rightarrow \infty\)</span>, the impact of the shrinkage penalty grows; when <span class="math inline">\(\lambda =0\)</span>, ridge regression produces least squares estimates. For each <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span>, ridge regression produces a different set of coefficient estimates. so selecting a good value for <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> is critical. </p> <p>when ridge regression has coefficient estimates shrinkun to 0, this correspond to the null model.</p> <p> term: <span class="math inline">\(||\hat{\beta}_\lambda^R||_2/||\hat{\beta}||_2 \in [0,1]\)</span>. here the notation <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\beta}\)</span> denotes the vector of least squares coefficient estimates; <span class="math inline">\(||\hat{\beta}||_2\)</span> denotes the <span class="math inline">\(\ell_2\)</span> norm of a vector, and is defined as <span class="math inline">\(||\beta||_2=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2}\)</span>, which measures the distance of <span class="math inline">\(\beta\)</span> from <span class="math inline">\((0,0,\dots, 0)_{p-1}\)</span>. </p> <p> as <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> increases, the <span class="math inline">\(\ell_2\)</span> norm of <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\beta}_\lambda^R\)</span> will always decrease, and so will <span class="math inline">\(||\hat{\beta}_\lambda^R||_2/||\hat{\beta}||_2\)</span>. when <span class="math inline">\(\lambda=0\)</span> when ridge regression penalty term equals RSS, the quantity equals 1; when <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \rightarrow \infty\)</span> and therefore the ridge regression coefficient estimate is a vector of 0s and <span class="math inline">\(\ell_2\)</span> norm equal to 0, the quantity equal to 0. A very small value of this quantity indicates that the ridge regression coefficient estimates have been shrunken towards 0. </p> <p> <strong>attention</strong>: ridge regression is sensitive to the scaling of predictors. In fact, the value of <span class="math inline">\(X_j\beta_{j,\lambda}^R\)</span> will depend not only on the value of <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span>, but also on the scaling of the <span class="math inline">\(j\)</span>th predictor. therefore, it’s best to apply ridge regression after standardizing the predictors so that all standardized predictors all have a standard deviation of 1. </p> <p>why does ridge regression improve over least squares?</p> <ul> <li> ridge regression’s advantage over least squares is rooted in the bias-variance trade-off. <ul> <li> as <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> increases, the flexibility of the ridge regression fit decreases, leading to decreased variance but increased bias. </li> <li> in general, when the relationship between the response and predictors is close to linear, the least squares estimates will have low bias but may have high variance, which means s small change in the training data can cause a large change in the least squares coefficient estimates. Particularly, when <span class="math inline">\(p \rightarrow n\)</span>, the least squares estimates will be extremely variable; if <span class="math inline">\(p > n\)</span>, then the least squares estimates do not even have a unique solution, whereas ridge regression can still perform well by trading off a small increase in bias for large decrease in variance. </li> <li>therefore, ridge regression works best when the least squares estimates have high variance.</li> <li> ridge regression had computational advantages over best subset selection, which requires search for <span class="math inline">\(2^p\)</span> models. in contrast, for a given <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span>, ridge regression fits only one model and it can be done very quickly. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p>disadvantages of ridge regression:</p> <ul> <li> unlike best subset, forward stepwise and backward stepwise selection which generally select models that contain a subset of predictors, ridge regression will include all predictors in the final model <ul> <li> the <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\)</span> will shrink all coefficient towards 0, but it will not set any of them exactly to 0 (unless <span class="math inline">\(\lambda = \infty\)</span>). </li> <li>it may not be a problem for prediction accuracy, but it causes problems to interpretation especially when p is large.</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="lasso" class="section level4"> <h4>lasso</h4> <p> lasso is a recent alternative to ridge regression that gets rid of noise variables: <span class="math display">\[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\beta_0-\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij})^2+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|=\rm RSS + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j| \]</span> comparing lasso to ridge regression, lasso has a similar formulation. the only difference is that we replace <span class="math inline">\(\beta_j^2\)</span> in the ridge regression penalty with <span class="math inline">\(|\beta_j|\)</span> in the lasso. in statistical parlance, lasso uses <span class="math inline">\(\ell_1\)</span> penalty instead of <span class="math inline">\(\ell_2\)</span> penalty. the <span class="math inline">\(\ell_1\)</span> norm of a coefficient vector <span class="math inline">\(\beta\)</span> is defined by <span class="math inline">\(||\beta||=\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\)</span>. </p> <p> like ridge regression, lasso shrinks the coefficient estimates towards 0. however, the <span class="math inline">\(\ell_1\)</span> penalty will force some of the coefficient estimates to be exactly 0 when the tuning parameter <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> is sufficiently large. Hence, much like best subset selection, the lasso performs <strong>variable selection</strong>. consequently, models generated from lasso are generally easier to interpret than those produced by ridge regression. </p> <p>we say lasso yields <strong>sparse</strong> models-that is, models that contain only a subset of predictors.</p> <ul> <li>when <span class="math inline">\(\lambda=0\)</span>, lass0 simply gives the least squares estimates</li> <li> when <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \rightarrow \infty\)</span>, lasso give the <em>null</em> model where every coefficient estimates are 0 </li> <li> in between two extremes, lasso is quite different from ridge regression, depending on the value of <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span>, lasso can produce a model involving any number of variables. </li> </ul> <p>re-formularize ridge regression and lasso <span class="math display">\[ \rm \]</span></p> <p> we can think of above equation as follows: when we perform lasso we are trying to find the set of coefficient estimates that lead to the smallest RSS, subject to the constraint that there is a budget of <span class="math inline">\(s\)</span> for how large <span class="math inline">\(\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\)</span> can be. </p> <ul> <li> when <span class="math inline">\(s\)</span> is extremely large, then this budget is not very restrictive, and the coefficient estimates can be large. in fact, if s is large enough that the least squares falls within the budget, then it will simply yield the least squares solution </li> <li>if s is small, then the penalty must be small to avoid violating the budget.</li> </ul> <div id="lasso-vs.-ridge-regression" class="section level5"> <h5>lasso vs. ridge regression</h5> <ul> <li>it is clear that lasso leads to simpler and more interpretable models than ridge regression.</li> <li>as <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> increases, there is a drop in variance in return of an increase in bias.</li> <li> but which one produces more accurate models or better prediction accuracy? <ul> <li>overall, neither ridge regression nor lasso will universally dominate the other.</li> <li> lasso will perform better in a setting where a relatively small number of predictors have substantial coefficients, and the remaining predictors have coefficients that are very small or 0. </li> <li> ridge regression will perform better when the response is a function of many predictors, all with coefficients of roughly equal size. </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="selecting-the-tuning-parameter" class="section level5"> <h5>selecting the tuning parameter</h5> <p> implementing ridge regression and lasso requires a method for selecting a value for the tuning parameter <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span>, or equivalently, the value of the constraint <strong>s</strong>. </p> <p> cross-validation provides a simple way to tackle this problem. we choose a grid of <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> values, and compute the cross-validation error for each value of <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span>. we then select the tuning parameter value doe which the cross-validation error is smallest. finally, the model is re-fit using all observations and the selected value of the tuning parameter. </p> </div> </div> </div> <div id="dimension-reduction-methods" class="section level3"> <h3>dimension reduction methods</h3> <p> subset selection and shrinkage method have controlled variance by using a subset of the original variables and shrinking their coefficients towards 0. all of these methods are defined using the original predictors. next we explore a class of approaches that transform the predictors and then fit a least squares model using the transformed variables. </p> <p> let <span class="math inline">\(Z_1, Z_2, \dots, Z_M\)</span> denote <span class="math inline">\(M < P\)</span> linear combinations of our original p predictors. that is <span class="math display">\[ Z_m=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_{jm}X_j \]</span> for some constraint <span class="math inline">\(\phi_{1m}, \phi_{2m}, \dots, \phi_{pm}, m=1,\dots,\rm M\)</span>. we can then fit the linear regression model <span class="math display">\[ y_i=\theta_0+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\theta_mz_{im}+\epsilon_i, i=1,\dots,n \]</span> using least squares. </p> <p> we can derive <span class="math display">\[ \beta_j=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\theta_m\phi_{jm} \]</span> here <span class="math inline">\(\phi_{jm}\)</span> are the principal component loadings, which defined the direction. </p> <p> in situations where p is large relative to n, selecting a value of <span class="math inline">\(M \ll p\)</span> can significantly reduce the variance of the fitted coefficients; if <span class="math inline">\(M=p\)</span>, then no dimension reduction occurs. </p> <p>all dimension reduction methods work in two steps:</p> <ul> <li>first, the transformed predictors are obtained.</li> <li>second, the model is fit using these M transformed predictors.</li> </ul> <p>however, we can choose different ways to transform the original predictors.</p> <div id="principal-components-regression" class="section level4"> <h4>principal components regression</h4> <p> The first principal component <span class="math inline">\(Z_1\)</span> direction of the data is that along which the observations vary the most. that is, if we project the observations onto this line, then then resulting projected observations would have the largest possible variance. </p> <p> the second principal component <span class="math inline">\(Z_2\)</span> is a linear combination of the variable that is uncorrelated with <span class="math inline">\(Z_1\)</span>, and has largest variance subject to this constraint. it turns out that zero correlation condition of two directions is equivalent to the condition that the direction must be perpendicular, or orthogonal, to the first principal component direction. </p> <p>advantages of PCR:</p> <ul> <li> PCR tends to do well in cases when the first few principal components are sufficient to capture most of the variation in the predictor as well as the relationship with the response. <ul> <li>when many principal components are required to adequately model the response, PCR performs worse.</li> <li>overall, <strong>PCR</strong> offers a significant improvement over <strong>least squares</strong></li> <li><strong>PCR</strong> and <strong>ridge regression</strong> slightly outperform <strong>lasso</strong>.</li> <li> PCR is not performing variable selection, since each principal component used in PCR is a linear combination of all the predictors. </li> <li>PCR and ridge regression are closely related.</li> </ul> </li> </ul> <p>disadvantage</p> <ul> <li> PCR suffers from a drawback: there is no guarantee that the directions that best explain the predictors will also be the best directions to use for predicting the response. </li> </ul> </div> <div id="partial-least-squares" class="section level4"> <h4>partial least squares</h4> <p> PCR involves identifying linear combinations, or directions, that best capture the variance. these directions are identified in an <strong>unsupervised</strong> way, since the response Y is not used to help determine the principal component directions. </p> <p> partial least squares(PLS) is an supervised alternative to PCR. likewise, PLS is a dimension reduction method, whcih first identifies a new set of features <span class="math inline">\(Z_1, \dots, Z_M\)</span> that are linear combinations of the original features, and then fits a linear model via least squares using these M new features. But unlike PCR, PLS identifies these new features in a supervised way with the response involved so tha the M new features are not only approximate the original features well, but also are related to the response. Overall, PLS attempts to find directions that help explain both the response and the predictors. </p> <p>implementation of PLS:</p> <ul> <li> <p> after standardizing all predictors, PLS computes the first direction <span class="math inline">\(Z_1\)</span> by setting each <span class="math inline">\(\phi_{j1}\)</span> equal to the coefficient fromthe simple linear regression of Y onto <span class="math inline">\(X_j\)</span>. Hence, in computing <span class="math inline">\(Z_1=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_{j1}X_J\)</span>, PLS places the highest weight on the variables that are most strongly related to the response. </p> </li> <li> <p>to identify the second PLS direction,</p> <ul> <li> we first adjust each of the variable for <span class="math inline">\(Z_1\)</span>, by regressing each variable on <span class="math inline">\(Z_1\)</span> and taking residuals. these residuals can be interpreted as the remaining information that has not been explained by the first PLS direction. </li> <li> we then compute <span class="math inline">\(Z_2\)</span> using this orthogonalized data in exactly the same fashion as <span class="math inline">\(Z_1\)</span> was computed based on the original data. </li> <li>this iterative approach can be repeated M times to identify multiple PLS components</li> <li>finally, we use least squares to fit a linear model to predict Y using all PLS components.</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> </div> <div id="high-dimension-considerations" class="section level3"> <h3>high-dimension considerations</h3> <p> terminology: data sets containing more features than observations are often referred to as <strong>high-dimensional</strong>. classical approaches such as least squares linear regression are not appropriate in this setting. </p> <div id="what-goes-wrong-in-high-dimensions" class="section level4"> <h4>what goes wrong in high dimensions?</h4> <p> for classical statistical methods, least squares for example, that are not intended for high-dimensional setting, when the number of features is as large as, or larger than, the number of observations <span class="math inline">\(p>n, \rm or, p \approx n\)</span>, least squares cannot be performed. the reason is that: </p> <ul> <li> regardless of whether or not there truly is a relationship between the features and the response, least squares will yield a set of coefficient estimates that result in a perfect fit to the data, such that the residuals are 0. <ul> <li>this is problematic because this perfect fit will almost certainly lead to over-fitting.</li> <li> that is although it’s possible to perfectly fit the training data in high-dimensional setting, the resulting linear model will perform extremely poor on an independent test set, and therefore does not constitute a useful model. </li> <li>thus a simple least squares regression line is too flexible and hence overfits the data.</li> <li><span class="math inline">\(R^2, C_p\)</span>, AIC, BIC are all not applicable in high-dimensional setting</li> </ul> </li> </ul> </div> <div id="regression-in-high-dimensions" class="section level4"> <h4>regression in high-dimensions</h4> <p> many of the methods introduced so
